questions.q: Which statement is one of the three original principles of the cell theory?
choices: New cells arise only from pre-existing cells by cell division.
Cells can arise spontaneously from nonliving matter when conditions are right.
All cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus.
Only multicellular organisms are made of cells.
questions.explain: The classic cell theory says all living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the smallest unit of life, and cells come only from pre-existing cells. Spontaneous generation is exactly the idea the theory rejected, and many cells (prokaryotes) have no nucleus.

questions.q: Which of the following is a modern addition to the cell theory?
choices: Cells contain hereditary information (DNA) that is passed from cell to cell during division.
Every cell contains mitochondria to supply its energy.
Cells are built mainly from carbohydrates rather than proteins.
Viruses are the simplest type of living cell.
questions.explain: Modern additions include that cells carry DNA passed on during division, that all cells have basically the same chemical composition, and that energy flow (metabolism) happens within cells. Mitochondria are not universal, since prokaryotes lack them, and viruses are not cells.

questions.q: Which set of features is shared by ALL cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic?
choices: Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material, and ribosomes
Nucleus, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and plasma membrane
Plasma membrane, cell wall, DNA, and mitochondria
Ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, DNA, and cytoplasm
questions.explain: Regardless of size or type, every cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material, and ribosomes. The most tempting wrong set includes a nucleus, but prokaryotes have no nucleus; their DNA sits in a nucleoid region.

questions.q: A newly discovered single-celled organism has DNA in a nucleoid region, ribosomes, a cell wall, and a plasma membrane, but no internal membrane-bound organelles. How should it be classified?
choices: As a prokaryote, because its DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus
As a eukaryote, because it has ribosomes
As a plant cell, because it has a cell wall
As a non-living particle, because it lacks mitochondria
questions.explain: A nucleoid and no membrane-bound organelles are the defining features of a prokaryote. Ribosomes and cell walls appear in both prokaryotes and some eukaryotes, so they do not identify a eukaryote or a plant.

questions.q: As a cell grows larger, what happens to its surface area-to-volume ratio, and why does it matter?
choices: The ratio increases, so the cell exchanges materials more efficiently.
The ratio stays the same because surface area and volume grow at the same rate.
The ratio decreases, which speeds up diffusion to the center of the cell.
The ratio decreases, so the membrane has relatively less area to take in nutrients and export wastes for the cell's volume.
questions.explain: Volume grows faster (cubed) than surface area (squared), so the ratio falls as cells enlarge. A high ratio is needed for adequate exchange, which is why cells stay small. A falling ratio slows exchange rather than speeding it up.

questions.q: Two cube-shaped cells are compared: one is 1 µm on a side, the other 10 µm on a side. Which cell is better suited for exchanging materials with its environment?
choices: The 1 µm cell, because its surface area-to-volume ratio is 10 times higher
The 10 µm cell, because it has 100 times more surface area
Both are equal, because they have the same shape
The 10 µm cell, because its larger volume holds more transport proteins
questions.explain: 1 µm cube: SA = 6, V = 1, ratio 6. 10 µm cube: SA = 600, V = 1000, ratio 0.6. The larger cell does have more total surface area, but it has far more volume to supply, so exchange per unit volume is worse.

questions.q: In a typical bacterial cell, where is the DNA located?
choices: In the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm
Inside a membrane-bound nucleus
In the nucleolus
In the glycocalyx outside the cell wall
questions.explain: Bacteria have no nucleus; their DNA is concentrated in a nucleoid region that is not enclosed by a membrane. The nucleolus is a structure inside a eukaryotic nucleus.

questions.q: Which bacterial structure is correctly matched with its function?
choices: Flagella: storing the cell's DNA
Glycocalyx: protein synthesis
Cell wall: site of ATP production by photosynthesis
Pili: attachment to surfaces or other cells
questions.explain: Pili are appendages used for attachment, while flagella are used for movement. The glycocalyx traps water, protects the cell, and can help it evade the immune system; ribosomes make proteins.

questions.q: How does the plasma membrane differ from a cell wall?
choices: The cell wall is selectively permeable, while the plasma membrane is a rigid support layer.
Only plant cells have a plasma membrane; animal cells have a cell wall instead.
They are the same structure described by two different names.
The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves; the cell wall is a rigid outer layer that gives support and protection.
questions.explain: Every cell has a plasma membrane that regulates transport, signaling, and adhesion. Cell walls (in bacteria, plants, fungi) sit outside the membrane and provide structural support. Animal cells have a plasma membrane but no cell wall.

questions.q: Which statement about archaea matches the lecture description?
choices: They are prokaryotes that are often found in extreme environments.
They are eukaryotes with a true nucleus.
They are typically about 100 µm in diameter, much larger than eukaryotic cells.
They are the most common cause of human disease.
questions.explain: Archaea are small (about 1 to 10 µm) prokaryotic cells, less common than bacteria, and often live in extreme habitats. They lack a nucleus. Disease-causing prokaryotes are mostly bacteria, and even most bacteria are harmless.

questions.q: A cell has a nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, and a cell wall. What kind of cell is it?
choices: An animal cell
A plant cell
A bacterial cell
An archaeal cell
questions.explain: A nucleus and organelles make it eukaryotic; chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, and a cell wall together point to a plant cell. Animal cells lack chloroplasts and cell walls, and bacteria and archaea lack a nucleus.

questions.q: Which statement is NOT a true difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
choices: Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotic cells do not.
Eukaryotic cells have internal membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells do not.
Eukaryotic cells have ribosomes, while prokaryotic cells lack them.
Prokaryotic cells are typically much smaller than eukaryotic cells.
questions.explain: Ribosomes are one of the four features shared by all cells, so they are not a difference. The nucleus, internal membrane-bound organelles, and size are real differences between the two cell types.

questions.q: A strain of bacteria with a thick capsule (glycocalyx) is cleared by the immune system much more slowly than a strain without one. What does this suggest about the glycocalyx?
choices: It protects the cell and helps it evade the host immune system.
It is the site where the bacterium makes ATP.
It lets the bacterium swim away from immune cells.
It stores the cell's genetic material.
questions.explain: The glycocalyx (capsule) traps water, protects the cell, and helps it evade the immune system. Swimming is the job of flagella, not the capsule.

questions.q: Which structure is NOT part of the endomembrane system?
choices: Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
Nuclear envelope
questions.explain: The endomembrane system includes the nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, vesicles, and plasma membrane. Mitochondria are semiautonomous organelles that are not connected to this membrane network by vesicle traffic.

questions.q: What do the organelles of the endomembrane system have in common?
choices: They each contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
They are all built from microtubules.
They are membrane-bound compartments that are connected directly or through vesicles that carry material between them.
They are all found in prokaryotic cells as well as eukaryotic cells.
questions.explain: Endomembrane organelles share membranes either by direct continuity (nuclear envelope with ER) or by vesicle transport. Having their own DNA and ribosomes describes mitochondria and chloroplasts, not the endomembrane system.

questions.q: What is the main function of the nucleolus?
choices: Making ribosomal RNA and assembling ribosomal subunits
Translating mRNA into proteins
Controlling traffic into and out of the nucleus through pores
Storing calcium ions for the cell
questions.explain: The nucleolus is a region inside the nucleus where rRNA is made and ribosomal subunits are assembled. Translation happens on ribosomes in the cytosol, and the nuclear envelope (with its pores) controls traffic in and out of the nucleus.

questions.q: Which description fits the nuclear envelope?
choices: A single membrane where most of the cell's lipids are made
A network of protein fibers that pulls chromosomes apart
A double membrane with pores that separates the nuclear contents from the cytoplasm
A region inside the nucleus where ribosomal subunits are assembled
questions.explain: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane perforated by nuclear pores that regulate what moves between nucleus and cytoplasm. The nucleolus, not the envelope, assembles ribosomal subunits.

questions.q: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?
choices: Chromatin is made of RNA, while chromosomes are made of DNA.
They are the same DNA-protein material; chromosomes are a more condensed form seen when a cell prepares to divide.
Chromatin is found only in prokaryotes, while chromosomes are found only in eukaryotes.
Chromosomes contain protein, but chromatin is DNA with no protein.
questions.explain: Chromatin is the DNA-protein complex in the nucleus; when cells prepare to divide, it condenses into compact chromosomes. Both are DNA plus protein (such as histones), just in different conformations.

questions.q: Where are ribosomes made, and where do they carry out protein synthesis?
choices: They are made in the Golgi apparatus and work inside the nucleus.
Their subunits are assembled in the nucleolus; they make proteins in the cytosol, either free or bound to the rough ER.
They are made in the cytosol and work only inside lysosomes.
They are made by the smooth ER and work inside the nucleolus.
questions.explain: Ribosomal subunits are built in the nucleolus, exported to the cytoplasm, and translate mRNA there, either free in the cytosol or attached to the rough ER. Proteins are not made inside the nucleus.

questions.q: Cells of the ovaries and testes produce and secrete large amounts of steroid hormones, which are lipids. Which organelle would you predict to be especially abundant in these cells?
choices: Rough ER, because its ribosomes make steroid hormones
Lysosomes, because they digest cholesterol into hormones
Smooth ER, because it synthesizes lipids
The central vacuole, because it stores hormones
questions.explain: Smooth ER synthesizes lipids, including steroids. Rough ER is tempting because it is linked to secretion, but its ribosomes make proteins, and steroids are lipids, not proteins.

questions.q: Liver cells break down toxins such as alcohol to clean the blood. Which organelle is chiefly responsible, and so likely abundant, in these cells?
choices: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Golgi apparatus
Nucleolus
questions.explain: Smooth ER functions include lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, calcium storage, and detoxifying poisons, so liver cells have a lot of it. Rough ER is mainly for making secreted and membrane proteins.

questions.q: Pancreatic cells make and secrete the protein hormone insulin. If a cell's Golgi apparatus stopped working, what would you predict?
choices: Insulin would no longer be translated, because the Golgi is where proteins are made.
Insulin would still be made at the rough ER but would not be properly processed, sorted, and packaged into secretory vesicles, so secretion would drop.
Insulin would be secreted faster, because it would skip a processing step.
Insulin would be sent to the nucleus instead of being secreted.
questions.explain: In the secretory pathway, proteins made by ribosomes on the rough ER travel in vesicles to the Golgi, which modifies, sorts, and packages them for secretion. Without the Golgi, synthesis continues but delivery to the plasma membrane fails. The Golgi does not make proteins.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces a secreted protein from synthesis to release from the cell?
choices: Golgi apparatus → rough ER → transport vesicle → lysosome → plasma membrane
Free ribosome → nucleus → Golgi apparatus → ER → plasma membrane
Ribosome on rough ER → ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
Smooth ER → lysosome → Golgi apparatus → transport vesicle → plasma membrane
questions.explain: Secreted proteins enter the ER as they are translated, bud off in transport vesicles to the Golgi, and leave the Golgi in secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane (exocytosis). The Golgi comes after the ER, not before it.

questions.q: Macrophages are white blood cells that engulf and destroy invading bacteria. Which organelle would be especially abundant in them?
choices: Chloroplasts
Smooth ER
Central vacuole
Lysosomes
questions.explain: Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes (acid hydrolases) that break down engulfed material, so cells that destroy bacteria need many of them. Smooth ER detoxifies chemicals but does not digest whole bacteria.

questions.q: Lysosomal enzymes are acid hydrolases that work best at about pH 5. If a lysosome's proton pumps failed and its interior rose to about pH 7, what would happen?
choices: Its digestive enzymes would work poorly, so breakdown of materials would slow.
Its enzymes would work faster, because pH 7 is neutral.
The lysosome would start producing ATP instead.
Nothing would change, because lysosomal enzymes are not affected by pH.
questions.explain: Proton pumps in the lysosomal membrane keep the inside acidic so the acid hydrolases work. Raising the pH moves them away from their optimum. Neutral pH is not better for enzymes that are adapted to an acidic environment.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes endocytosis from exocytosis?
choices: Exocytosis takes material into the cell; endocytosis releases material from the cell.
Endocytosis takes material into the cell when the plasma membrane folds inward to form a vesicle; exocytosis releases material when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.
Both describe small molecules diffusing directly through the lipid bilayer.
Endocytosis releases waste from the cell, and exocytosis builds new organelles.
questions.explain: Endo- means 'into': the membrane pinches inward around material to form a vesicle. Exo- means 'out of': a vesicle fuses with the membrane and empties its contents outside. Neither one is simple diffusion.

questions.q: What is a main role of the large central vacuole in a plant cell?
choices: Storing water and solutes and maintaining turgor pressure that helps support the cell
Producing ATP using light energy
Synthesizing proteins for export
Forming microtubules during cell division
questions.explain: The central vacuole stores water, ions, and other materials. When it is full, it presses the cytoplasm against the wall (turgor), which keeps plant tissues firm. Chloroplasts capture light energy, and ribosomes make proteins.

questions.q: Why is the rough ER called 'rough'?
choices: It contains stacked thylakoids.
Its membrane is studded with cholesterol crystals.
It is coated with microtubules.
Ribosomes are bound to its cytosolic surface.
questions.explain: Bound ribosomes give the rough ER its studded look. These ribosomes make proteins (including glycoproteins) that enter the ER for membranes, organelles, or secretion. Thylakoids are found in chloroplasts.

questions.q: Which description best fits the Golgi apparatus?
choices: A double-membrane organelle that makes ATP
A network of protein fibers that gives the cell its shape
Stacks of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) that modify, sort, and package proteins and lipids received from the ER
A single sac of acid hydrolases that digests worn-out organelles
questions.explain: The Golgi is made of stacked cisternae that receive ER products in transport vesicles, modify them, and send them to their destinations. The sac of acid hydrolases describes a lysosome.

questions.q: A protein that is normally secreted is engineered so that its ER signal sequence is deleted. What is the most likely result?
choices: It is secreted faster than normal.
It is automatically sent into the nucleus.
It is translated by a free ribosome and stays in the cytosol instead of entering the ER.
It cannot be translated at all.
questions.explain: In cotranslational sorting, the signal recognition particle binds the ER signal sequence and brings the ribosome to the ER. Without that signal, the protein is finished in the cytosol and never enters the secretory pathway. Translation itself still happens.

questions.q: Most proteins destined for mitochondria, chloroplasts, the nucleus, and peroxisomes are sorted in which way?
choices: Cotranslationally: they are made on the rough ER and delivered through the Golgi.
They are made inside the Golgi apparatus itself.
Post-translationally: they are completed in the cytosol and then imported, guided by a short sorting sequence.
They are made by the nucleolus and released into the target organelle.
questions.explain: Post-translational sorting applies to proteins for the nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes: they are made in the cytosol and taken up using a short targeting sequence, sometimes kept unfolded by chaperones. ER, Golgi, lysosome, plasma membrane, and secreted proteins use cotranslational sorting.

questions.q: Which description fits mitochondrial structure?
choices: An outer membrane and a highly folded inner membrane that surrounds a fluid matrix
A single membrane enclosing digestive enzymes
An inner membrane enclosing stroma with stacks of thylakoids
Hollow tubes built from tubulin
questions.explain: Mitochondria have a double membrane, with the inner one folded to increase the surface for making ATP. Stroma and thylakoids belong to chloroplasts, and a single membrane holding digestive enzymes describes a lysosome.

questions.q: Which description fits chloroplast structure?
choices: A single membrane with folds called cristae
A double membrane; the inner membrane encloses fluid stroma containing grana, which are stacks of thylakoids
Stacked cisternae that package proteins
A cluster of ribosomes with no membrane
questions.explain: Chloroplasts are double-membrane organelles; inside the stroma are grana made of stacked, hollow thylakoid sacs, where light is captured. Stacked cisternae describe the Golgi.

questions.q: A hummingbird beats its wings dozens of times per second for long periods. Which organelle would you expect to be especially abundant in its flight muscle cells?
choices: Lysosomes
Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
Golgi apparatus
questions.explain: Constant, intense contraction demands a lot of ATP, and mitochondria are the main site of ATP production. Animal cells have no chloroplasts, and the Golgi is for processing and shipping proteins, not energy.

questions.q: Cells in the upper layer of a leaf receive the most sunlight. Which organelle would you predict to be most abundant in them compared with root cells?
choices: Lysosomes
Rough ER
Chloroplasts
Centrioles
questions.explain: Chloroplasts capture light energy for photosynthesis, so cells that receive the most light pack in the most chloroplasts. Plant cells lack centrioles altogether.

questions.q: Cells lining the stomach make and secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes, which are proteins. If these cells lost most of their rough ER, which process would fail most directly?
choices: Detoxification of drugs and alcohol
Production of the digestive enzymes they secrete
Synthesis of steroid hormones
Capture of light energy
questions.explain: Secreted proteins are made by ribosomes bound to the rough ER, so losing it would cripple enzyme production and secretion. Detoxification and steroid synthesis are smooth ER jobs.

questions.q: A mutation leaves a muscle cell with very few working mitochondria. What is the most direct consequence?
choices: The cell would no longer be able to translate proteins.
Greatly reduced aerobic ATP production, so the cell would struggle to sustain contraction
The cell would lose its ability to digest engulfed bacteria.
The cell's DNA would no longer be enclosed by a nucleus.
questions.explain: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP using oxygen-requiring (aerobic) reactions. Muscle contraction is ATP-hungry, so energy supply fails first. Translation depends on ribosomes and digestion on lysosomes.

questions.q: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts called 'semiautonomous'?
choices: They are fully independent organisms that can survive outside the cell.
They grow and divide on their own, but depend on the cell to make many of their components.
They cannot divide and must be built new by the ER.
They are found only in prokaryotic cells.
questions.explain: These organelles reproduce by growth and division, but they are not fully independent because they rely on the cell for synthesis of many internal components (many of their proteins are encoded in the nucleus and imported).

questions.q: According to the endosymbiosis theory presented in class, what were the ancestors of mitochondria and chloroplasts?
choices: Mitochondria came from cyanobacteria; chloroplasts came from purple bacteria.
Both came from archaea living in extreme environments.
Mitochondria came from purple bacteria (α-proteobacteria); chloroplasts came from cyanobacteria.
Both formed when pieces of the ER pinched off and became specialized.
questions.explain: Endosymbiosis is a smaller species living inside a larger one. Mitochondria descend from purple bacteria and chloroplasts from photosynthetic cyanobacteria. Swapping the two is the most common mix-up; it helps to remember that cyanobacteria photosynthesize, like chloroplasts.

questions.q: Which observation best supports the idea that mitochondria and chloroplasts arose by endosymbiosis?
choices: They receive proteins from the ER through vesicles.
They are present in every prokaryotic cell.
They have their own DNA and ribosomes and divide in a way similar to bacteria.
They are built from tubulin, like microtubules.
questions.explain: Their own genetic material, ribosomes, and bacterium-like division suggest they were once free-living prokaryotes. Prokaryotes do not contain mitochondria or chloroplasts, and these organelles are not part of the vesicle-connected endomembrane system.

questions.q: Cells in a plant root grow underground, in the dark. Compared with leaf cells, which organelle would you expect them to have few or none of?
choices: Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
Nucleus
Ribosomes
questions.explain: Chloroplasts are needed only where light is captured, so root cells have essentially none. Root cells still need mitochondria to make ATP, plus a nucleus and ribosomes like any plant cell.

questions.q: A student says plant cells do not need mitochondria because they have chloroplasts. What is the best response?
choices: That is correct: chloroplasts replace mitochondria in plants.
That is wrong: plant cells have both. Chloroplasts use light energy to make sugars, and mitochondria break down sugars to make ATP.
That is wrong: plant cells have mitochondria but not chloroplasts.
That is correct: plants get all their ATP directly from sunlight in the vacuole.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar; cells, including plant cells, still need mitochondria to convert that sugar into ATP. Thinking that chloroplasts replace mitochondria is a very common misconception.

questions.q: A sperm cell swims a long distance using its flagellum. Which organelle would you expect to be concentrated near the base of the flagellum?
choices: Chloroplasts, to capture light for movement
The central vacuole, to store water for movement
Smooth ER, to make lipids for movement
Mitochondria, to supply ATP for movement
questions.explain: Flagellar beating is driven by dynein motor proteins that use ATP, so mitochondria cluster where the energy is needed. Animal cells such as sperm lack chloroplasts and a central vacuole.

questions.q: Gland cells secrete large amounts of a protein hormone. Which pair of organelles would you expect to be most extensive in them?
choices: Smooth ER and lysosomes
Chloroplasts and the central vacuole
Rough ER and Golgi apparatus
Centrioles and peroxisomes
questions.explain: Protein hormones are made on the rough ER, then processed and packaged by the Golgi for secretion. Smooth ER would matter more for a lipid (steroid) hormone.

questions.q: Which pair of organelles is each enclosed by a double membrane?
choices: Mitochondria and chloroplasts
Lysosomes and Golgi apparatus
Ribosomes and centrioles
Central vacuole and smooth ER
questions.explain: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both have an outer and an inner membrane, which fits their origin as engulfed bacteria. Lysosomes, the Golgi, vacuoles, and ER have single membranes, and ribosomes and centrioles have no membrane at all.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three main components of the cytoskeleton?
choices: Microtubules
Cisternae
Intermediate filaments
Actin filaments (microfilaments)
questions.explain: The cytoskeleton is made of microtubules, intermediate filaments, and actin filaments. Cisternae are the flattened membrane sacs of the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: Microtubules are best described as which of the following?
choices: Rope-like fibers made of keratin that bear tension
Long, hollow cylinders built from α- and β-tubulin, with a plus end and a minus end
Thin, solid fibers made of actin just under the plasma membrane
Flattened membrane sacs that move proteins
questions.explain: Microtubules are hollow tubes of α- and β-tubulin with distinct ends. Keratin ropes are intermediate filaments, and thin actin fibers are microfilaments.

questions.q: What does 'dynamic instability' of microtubules mean?
choices: A single microtubule can switch back and forth between growing and shrinking.
Microtubules are permanent and never change length once formed.
Microtubules break apart only when a cell dies.
Microtubules turn into intermediate filaments under stress.
questions.explain: Dynamic instability lets a microtubule alternate between growth and shortening phases, so the cell can rapidly rebuild its microtubule network, for example when forming the spindle for division.

questions.q: Which statement about microtubule-organizing centers (MTOCs) is correct?
choices: Plant cells use centrioles as their MTOC, but animal cells do not.
Animal cells use a centrosome containing centrioles as their MTOC; plant cells lack centrosomes and centrioles.
MTOCs are where actin filaments are assembled from tubulin.
MTOCs are found only in bacteria.
questions.explain: The MTOC is where microtubules grow from. In animals this is the centrosome with its centrioles; plants organize microtubules without centrioles.

questions.q: Skin cells must resist constant stretching and pulling. Which cytoskeletal component would be most important for this?
choices: Microtubules, because they are hollow
Intermediate filaments, such as keratins
Cilia, because they beat
Actin filaments, because they form the spindle
questions.explain: Intermediate filaments form rope-like, tension-bearing fibers that maintain cell shape and rigidity. Keratins are the classic example in skin. The spindle is made of microtubules, not actin.

questions.q: Actin filaments are also known as what?
choices: Microtubules
Nuclear lamins
Microfilaments
Centrioles
questions.explain: Actin filaments are called microfilaments. They support the plasma membrane and help determine cell shape and strength. Nuclear lamins are intermediate filaments.

questions.q: A drug prevents microtubules from assembling. If added to dividing cells, what would most likely happen?
choices: Ribosomes would stop translating mRNA.
Chromosomes could not be moved apart properly, so cell division would stall.
The plasma membrane would become fully permeable to ions.
Mitochondria would begin photosynthesis.
questions.explain: Microtubules move chromosomes during cell division (and form cilia and flagella). Blocking their assembly stops chromosome separation. Translation and membrane permeability do not depend directly on microtubules.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the cytoskeleton?
choices: Providing structural support
Storing the cell's genetic information
Transporting organelles within the cell
Helping the cell move and divide
questions.explain: The cytoskeleton provides support, aids cell division, transports organelles, and drives cell movement. Genetic information is stored in DNA, which is found mainly in the nucleus.

questions.q: How do cilia and flagella generally differ?
choices: Flagella are short and numerous; cilia are long and usually single.
Cilia are made of actin, while flagella are made of tubulin.
Cilia are found only in prokaryotes, and flagella only in eukaryotes.
Cilia are short and usually numerous, beating back and forth; flagella are longer, usually few, and move with a whip-like, wave motion.
questions.explain: Both are built from microtubules, but cilia are short and many, while flagella are long and few, with a different beating pattern. Saying they are made of different proteins is a common mistake; both use microtubules.

questions.q: What causes a cilium or eukaryotic flagellum to bend?
choices: Actin filaments contract around the base of the cilium.
Water rushes into the cilium by osmosis.
The motor protein dynein makes neighboring microtubules slide against each other.
Intermediate filaments inside the cilium shorten.
questions.explain: Dynein uses ATP to walk along an adjacent microtubule. Because the microtubules are linked, the sliding is converted into bending. Actin contraction drives other movements, such as muscle contraction, not ciliary bending.

questions.q: Paramecium is a single-celled organism covered in cilia. The cells lining the human airway are also ciliated. How do the roles of their cilia differ?
choices: Paramecium uses cilia to move itself through water; airway cells are anchored in tissue and use cilia to move mucus and particles past them.
Both use cilia only to move the whole cell through fluid.
Airway cilia move the cells through the lungs, while Paramecium cilia move water past a fixed cell.
Neither uses cilia for movement; cilia are used only for sensing.
questions.explain: Free-living ciliated cells live in aquatic environments and use cilia to swim. In multicellular tissues, cells stay in place and their cilia move the surrounding fluid, such as mucus, instead.

questions.q: A person inherits a defect in the dynein of their airway cilia. What would you predict?
choices: Airway cells would make more ATP.
The cilia cannot beat effectively, so mucus and trapped particles build up in the airways.
The cilia would beat faster to compensate.
Airway cells would lose their plasma membranes.
questions.explain: Without working dynein, microtubules cannot slide, so the cilia cannot bend and clear mucus. That leads to mucus buildup and frequent respiratory infections.

questions.q: Vesicles carrying proteins from the Golgi to the plasma membrane are moved through the cytoplasm mainly by what?
choices: Diffusion through nuclear pores
Contraction of intermediate filaments
Motor proteins that 'walk' along cytoskeletal tracks such as microtubules
Beating of cilia on the cell surface
questions.explain: The cytoskeleton acts as a network of tracks, and motor proteins use ATP to carry vesicles and organelles along them. Cilia move fluid outside the cell, not vesicles inside it.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the structure of an atom?
choices: Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus; electrons (−) occupy shells around it.
Electrons and protons are in the nucleus; neutrons orbit around it.
Neutrons are negatively charged and balance the protons.
Protons occupy shells around a nucleus made of electrons.
questions.explain: The nucleus holds the positive protons and neutral neutrons, while negatively charged electrons occupy shells outside. Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot balance the protons; the electrons do that.

questions.q: An atom has atomic number 8 and atomic mass 16. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: Atomic number = number of protons (8). Atomic mass = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8. Answering 16 confuses atomic mass with neutron number.

questions.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. How do they differ?
choices: In their number of neutrons
In their number of protons
In their number of electrons when neutral
They are different elements with different chemical properties
questions.explain: Isotopes are forms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. If the number of protons changed, it would be a different element.

questions.q: Which of the following is an element?
choices: Water (H₂O)
Methane (CH₄)
Table salt (NaCl)
Oxygen (O)
questions.explain: An element is a substance that cannot be broken down by chemical means into other substances. Water, methane, and salt are compounds made of two or more elements bonded together.

questions.q: How many electrons does a complete innermost shell hold, and how many do the outer shells of the atoms common in biology hold when complete?
choices: 8 in the innermost shell; 2 in outer shells
2 in every shell
4 in the innermost shell; 8 in outer shells
2 in the innermost shell; 8 in outer shells
questions.explain: The first shell is full with 2 electrons. For the outer shells of biologically important atoms, 8 electrons makes a full, stable valence shell (the octet).

questions.q: Phosphorus has atomic number 15. How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.explain: 15 electrons fill the shells as 2, 8, 5, so the outermost (valence) shell has 5. Answering 15 counts all electrons rather than only those in the outer shell.

questions.q: Nitrogen has atomic number 7. How many covalent bonds does it typically form?
questions.explain: Nitrogen's electrons are arranged 2, 5. It needs 3 more electrons to complete its octet, so it forms 3 covalent bonds (as in NH₃). The 5 valence electrons are not the number of bonds; the number of vacancies is.

questions.q: Neon (atomic number 10) is chemically inert. Why?
choices: It has no electrons.
Its valence shell is completely filled (2, 8), so it has no vacancies to fill by bonding.
Its nucleus has no protons.
It has only one electron in its valence shell.
questions.explain: Atoms are most stable when their outer shell has no vacancies. Neon's 10 electrons fill both the first (2) and second (8) shells, so it has no tendency to react. An atom with a single valence electron, like sodium, is very reactive.

questions.q: Why can carbon form up to four covalent bonds?
choices: It has 4 valence electrons, so it needs 4 more to complete its outer shell.
It has 4 protons in its nucleus.
It has 4 electron shells.
It has a full outer shell of 4 electrons.
questions.explain: The number of covalent bonds an atom forms is set by how many electrons it needs to fill its valence shell. Carbon (2, 4) needs four more, so it forms four bonds. Carbon has 6 protons, not 4.

questions.q: How many electrons are shared in a single covalent bond and in a double covalent bond?
choices: Single: 1 electron; double: 2 electrons
Single: 4 electrons; double: 8 electrons
Single: 2 electrons (one pair); double: 4 electrons (two pairs)
Single: 2 electrons; double: 3 electrons
questions.explain: A single covalent bond shares one pair (2 electrons); a double bond shares two pairs (4 electrons). Counting electrons rather than pairs is the usual source of error.

questions.q: What is electronegativity, and how does it affect the kind of bond that forms?
choices: It is the number of protons in an atom; atoms with equal electronegativity form ionic bonds.
It is the charge of an ion; atoms with high electronegativity always form nonpolar bonds.
It is an atom's ability to attract electrons; the larger the difference between two atoms, the more unequally electrons are shared, up to complete transfer in an ionic bond.
It is the mass of an atom; heavier atoms always form hydrogen bonds.
questions.explain: Similar electronegativities lead to equal sharing (nonpolar covalent bonds), moderate differences to unequal sharing (polar covalent bonds), and very large differences to electron transfer (ionic bonds). Equal electronegativity gives nonpolar covalent bonds, not ionic ones.

questions.q: Electronegativity values: C = 2.55, H = 2.20, N = 3.04, O = 3.44. Using the class cutoffs (difference < 0.45 is nonpolar covalent, 0.45 to 1.7 is polar covalent), which bond is nonpolar covalent?
choices: O–H
N–H
C–O
C–H
questions.explain: C–H: 2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35, below 0.45, so it is nonpolar. O–H (1.24), N–H (0.84), and C–O (0.89) all fall in the polar range. This is why hydrocarbons are nonpolar while molecules with O–H groups are polar.

questions.q: Sodium has an electronegativity of 0.93 and chlorine 3.16. What kind of interaction forms between them, and what happens to the electrons?
choices: A nonpolar covalent bond: the electrons are shared equally.
A polar covalent bond: the electrons are shared but sit closer to sodium.
A hydrogen bond: sodium's partial positive charge is attracted to chlorine.
An ionic bond: chlorine pulls an electron completely away from sodium, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other.
questions.explain: The difference (2.23) is greater than 1.7, so the electron is transferred rather than shared, producing a cation and an anion held by opposite charges. In any unequal sharing, the electrons would sit closer to the more electronegative atom (Cl), not to Na.

questions.q: An atom loses one electron. What does it become?
choices: An anion with a −1 charge
A cation with a +1 charge
An isotope with one fewer neutron
A neutral atom of a different element
questions.explain: Losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive (a cation, like Na⁺). Gaining an electron makes an anion. The element does not change, because the number of protons is unchanged.

questions.q: What is a hydrogen bond?
choices: A covalent bond in which two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons
A weak attraction between a partially positive hydrogen (covalently bonded to O or N) and a partially negative atom elsewhere
The complete transfer of an electron to a hydrogen atom
The strong bond that holds hydrogen to oxygen within a single water molecule
questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds come from polar covalent bonds: H bonded to a highly electronegative atom carries δ+, which is attracted to a δ− atom on another molecule or another part of the same molecule. The O–H bond inside a water molecule is a polar covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.

questions.q: In an O–P bond, oxygen is moderately more electronegative than phosphorus. Where are the shared electrons, and how are the partial charges arranged?
choices: The electrons sit closer to P, so P is δ− and O is δ+.
The electrons are shared equally, so there are no partial charges.
The electrons sit closer to O, so O is δ− and P is δ+.
The electrons are fully transferred to O, forming O²⁻ and P⁵⁺.
questions.explain: Shared electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative atom, giving it a partial negative charge. A moderate difference produces a polar covalent bond, not complete transfer.

questions.q: Which two elements common in cells are the most electronegative?
choices: Oxygen and nitrogen
Carbon and hydrogen
Hydrogen and phosphorus
Carbon and sulfur
questions.explain: O (3.44) and N (3.04) have the highest electronegativities among the common elements of life. That is why O–H and N–H bonds are polar and take part in hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Which four elements make up more than 96% of the human body?
choices: Oxygen, carbon, calcium, and iron
Carbon, hydrogen, sodium, and chlorine
Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen
Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and sulfur
questions.explain: The 'Big 4' are O, C, H, and N. Elements like calcium, phosphorus, and potassium are essential but present in much smaller amounts.

questions.q: What must a molecule contain to be considered organic, as defined in class?
choices: Oxygen and nitrogen
Phosphorus and sulfur
Sodium and chlorine
Carbon and hydrogen
questions.explain: Organic molecules are carbon-based compounds containing C and H. Methane (CH₄) is organic; water and NaCl are not.

questions.q: Water molecules stick to each other, which produces surface tension. What property is this, and what causes it?
choices: Adhesion, caused by covalent bonds between water molecules
Cohesion, caused by ionic bonds between oxygen atoms
Specific heat, caused by nonpolar bonds within water
Cohesion, caused by hydrogen bonds between water molecules
questions.explain: Cohesion is water sticking to water through hydrogen bonds between its polar molecules. Adhesion is water sticking to other surfaces. The covalent bonds are inside each water molecule, not between molecules.

questions.q: Water climbs a little way up the inside of a narrow glass tube. Which property mainly explains this?
choices: Adhesion: water molecules are attracted to the polar surface of the glass.
Cohesion alone: water molecules attract only each other.
High specific heat: the tube warms and pulls the water up.
Hydrophobic exclusion: the glass repels the water upward.
questions.explain: Adhesion is attraction between water and other polar or charged surfaces. Cohesion helps by pulling neighboring water molecules along, but the climb up the wall starts with adhesion to the glass.

questions.q: What is specific heat?
choices: The temperature at which a substance boils
The amount of heat released when a substance freezes
The amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C
The density of a substance at room temperature
questions.explain: Water has a high specific heat because much of the added energy goes into breaking hydrogen bonds before the molecules move faster. So water resists temperature changes.

questions.q: Coastal cities usually have milder temperatures than inland cities at the same latitude. Which property of water best explains this?
choices: Its low density lets ocean water float above the land.
Its adhesion makes the air stick to the coast.
Its high specific heat lets the ocean absorb and release large amounts of heat with little change in its own temperature.
Its nonpolar nature keeps heat out of the water.
questions.explain: Because hydrogen bonds make water resist temperature change, large bodies of water buffer nearby air temperatures in summer and winter. Water is polar, not nonpolar.

questions.q: Why does sweating cool the body?
choices: Hydrogen bonds must be broken for water to evaporate, and that energy is absorbed as heat from the skin.
Sweat contains salts that chemically absorb heat.
Water forms new covalent bonds with the skin, which releases cold.
Sweat is less dense than skin, so it carries heat upward.
questions.explain: Evaporation takes the fastest, most energetic molecules out of the liquid, and breaking their hydrogen bonds draws heat from the body surface. That is evaporative cooling, a consequence of water's hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Why does ice float on liquid water, and why does this matter for aquatic life?
choices: Ice is denser than water, so lakes freeze from the bottom up and protect fish.
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open lattice that is less dense than liquid water, so ice forms a floating layer that insulates the water beneath.
Ice contains trapped air from photosynthesis, so it floats.
Ice has fewer hydrogen bonds than liquid water, so it is lighter.
questions.explain: Water expands as it freezes because hydrogen bonds lock the molecules farther apart. The floating ice insulates liquid water below, so aquatic organisms survive the winter. Ice actually has more stable hydrogen bonds, not fewer.

questions.q: Which substance would you predict to be hydrophobic?
choices: A hydrocarbon made only of C–C and C–H bonds
Table salt (NaCl)
Glucose, which has many –OH groups
An amino acid with a charged side chain
questions.explain: C–C and C–H bonds are nonpolar, so a hydrocarbon has no partial charges for water to attract, and it does not dissolve. Ions, polar molecules with –OH groups, and charged molecules are hydrophilic.

questions.q: When table salt dissolves in water, how are water molecules arranged around a sodium ion (Na⁺)?
choices: The partially positive hydrogen atoms of water face the Na⁺.
Water molecules form covalent bonds with the Na⁺.
Water molecules are pushed away because Na⁺ is hydrophobic.
The partially negative oxygen atoms of water face the Na⁺.
questions.explain: Opposite charges attract: water's δ− oxygen faces cations like Na⁺, while its δ+ hydrogens face anions like Cl⁻. This shell of water helps keep ions dissolved.

questions.q: Why is a water molecule polar?
choices: Hydrogen is more electronegative than oxygen, so the H atoms are partially negative.
Water is held together by ionic bonds between H⁺ and O²⁻.
Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so shared electrons sit closer to O, making O partially negative and the H atoms partially positive.
Water's electrons are shared equally, but the molecule carries a net charge.
questions.explain: Unequal sharing in the polar covalent O–H bonds gives water partial charges. The molecule as a whole is neutral; it is the uneven distribution of charge that makes it polar.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the bonds within and between water molecules?
choices: Hydrogen bonds within each molecule; polar covalent bonds between molecules
Ionic bonds within each molecule; nonpolar covalent bonds between molecules
Nonpolar covalent bonds within each molecule; ionic bonds between molecules
Polar covalent bonds within each molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
questions.explain: Each H is joined to O by a strong polar covalent bond. The resulting partial charges let neighboring molecules attract through weaker hydrogen bonds. Mixing up these two levels is a frequent exam error.

questions.q: Water participates directly as a reactant in which kind of reaction?
choices: Dehydration synthesis, which builds polymers from monomers
Formation of a peptide bond
Formation of an ester bond in a triglyceride
Hydrolysis, which breaks polymers into monomers
questions.explain: Hydrolysis adds a water molecule to split a bond. Dehydration reactions, including peptide and ester bond formation, release water rather than consuming it. Water is also a reactant in photosynthesis.

questions.q: A plant pigment is nonpolar and will not dissolve in water. Which solvent would most likely dissolve it?
choices: Salt water, because ions attract the pigment
Hot water, because heat makes any substance dissolve in water
Sugar water, because sugar is a good solvent
A nonpolar solvent, such as vegetable oil
questions.explain: 'Like dissolves like': hydrophobic, nonpolar substances dissolve in nonpolar solvents, while hydrophilic substances dissolve in water. Heating water does not make it able to dissolve nonpolar molecules.

questions.q: If water could no longer form hydrogen bonds, which change would you predict?
choices: It would become a better solvent for nonpolar molecules.
It would become more cohesive.
Its temperature would rise and fall much more easily, because it would lose its high specific heat.
Ice would become even less dense.
questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds are behind cohesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling, and floating ice. Without them, water would heat and cool quickly and would lose its cohesion; ice would no longer have the open lattice that makes it float.

questions.q: Which description best fits lipids as a group?
choices: Polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
Carbon-containing compounds found in organisms that are largely nonpolar and hydrophobic
Polymers of nucleotides that store genetic information
Highly polar molecules that dissolve easily in water
questions.explain: Lipids are defined by being largely nonpolar and hydrophobic, not by having a single type of monomer. Amino acid and nucleotide polymers are proteins and nucleic acids.

questions.q: A triglyceride (fat) is formed from which components, joined by which bond?
choices: One glycerol and two fatty acids plus a phosphate, joined by peptide bonds
Three glucose molecules joined by hydrogen bonds
One glycerol and three fatty acids, joined by ester bonds formed through dehydration
Four fused carbon rings joined by ionic bonds
questions.explain: Triglycerides form when glycerol reacts with three fatty acids in dehydration reactions that create ester bonds. Glycerol plus two fatty acids plus a phosphate describes a phospholipid; four fused rings is a steroid.

questions.q: Why are saturated fats usually solid at room temperature while unsaturated fats are usually liquid?
choices: Saturated fats contain more double bonds, which lock molecules together.
Unsaturated fats are heavier, so they flow more easily.
Saturated fatty acid tails are straight and pack tightly; double bonds in unsaturated tails create kinks that prevent tight packing.
Saturated fats are polar and form hydrogen bonds with water.
questions.explain: Saturated means every carbon holds the most hydrogens possible, with no C=C double bonds, so the chains are straight. Cis double bonds bend the chain, and the bends keep molecules apart, so the fat stays liquid (an oil). The double bonds are in the unsaturated fats, not the saturated ones.

questions.q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. What is the best explanation?
choices: Butter is rich in saturated fatty acids, while olive oil is rich in unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds.
Butter is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, while olive oil is rich in saturated ones.
Butter is made of phospholipids, while olive oil is made of steroids.
Olive oil contains more hydrogen atoms per carbon than butter.
questions.explain: Animal fats are usually saturated and solid; plant fats are usually unsaturated and liquid. Unsaturated fats have fewer hydrogens per carbon because of their double bonds.

questions.q: An enzyme removes hydrogen atoms from a saturated fatty acid tail, creating a C=C double bond (dehydrogenation). How would this change the lipid?
choices: It becomes more saturated and more likely to be solid.
It turns into a steroid with four fused rings.
It becomes more unsaturated and kinked, and is more likely to be liquid at room temperature.
It becomes polar and fully water-soluble.
questions.explain: Removing hydrogens adds double bonds, which is the definition of unsaturation. The kink lowers how tightly molecules pack. The tail remains a hydrocarbon, so it stays nonpolar.

questions.q: Which statement about cis and trans fats matches the lecture?
choices: Trans fats occur naturally in all plant oils and are considered healthy.
Cis fats contain no double bonds.
Cis double bonds occur naturally; trans fats are mostly formed artificially and are linked to disease.
Trans and cis fats differ in how many fatty acids are attached to glycerol.
questions.explain: Natural unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds that kink the chain. Industrial processing creates trans fats, which are linked to cardiovascular disease. Both still have three fatty acids per triglyceride.

questions.q: How does a phospholipid differ from a fat (triglyceride)?
choices: A phospholipid has three fatty acids; a fat has two.
A phospholipid has no glycerol; a fat has two glycerols.
A phospholipid is a steroid ring; a fat is a chain of amino acids.
A phospholipid has glycerol, two fatty acids, and a phosphate-containing head group; a fat has glycerol and three fatty acids.
questions.explain: Replacing one fatty acid with a polar phosphate group gives the phospholipid a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, which is why phospholipids form membranes while fats store energy.

questions.q: What does it mean for a molecule to be amphipathic?
choices: It is entirely hydrophobic.
It is entirely hydrophilic.
It has both a hydrophilic (polar) region and a hydrophobic (nonpolar) region.
It can act as both an acid and a base.
questions.explain: Phospholipids are the classic amphipathic molecules: the phosphate head is polar and hydrophilic, while the fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic.

questions.q: Which of the following is a steroid?
choices: Cholesterol
A triglyceride
A phospholipid
A saturated fatty acid
questions.explain: Steroids are lipids with four fused carbon rings; cholesterol, estrogen, and testosterone are examples. Triglycerides, phospholipids, and fatty acids are built on chains rather than rings.

questions.q: Which describes biological functions of steroids?
choices: They act as hormones, such as estrogen and testosterone, and cholesterol helps regulate membrane fluidity.
They are the main enzymes that catalyze metabolic reactions.
They store the genetic code for proteins.
They form the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA.
questions.explain: Steroid hormones carry signals, and cholesterol in animal membranes buffers fluidity across temperatures. Catalysis is mainly done by proteins (enzymes), and genetic information is stored in nucleic acids.

questions.q: A lipid extracted from plant seeds is liquid at 25 °C. What is the most likely description of its fatty acids?
choices: Mostly saturated, with no double bonds
Mostly steroid rings
Mostly unsaturated, with cis double bonds
Mostly trans fats formed naturally
questions.explain: Plant fats are usually unsaturated, and the kinks from cis double bonds keep them liquid at room temperature. Trans fats are mostly made artificially, not by seeds.

questions.q: How many water molecules are released when one triglyceride is assembled from glycerol and fatty acids?
questions.explain: Each of the three fatty acids is attached to glycerol by a separate dehydration reaction that forms an ester bond and releases one H₂O, for 3 water molecules in total.

questions.q: Which class of biological molecules is NOT built as a polymer of repeating monomer units?
choices: Proteins
Nucleic acids
Lipids
Carbohydrates such as starch
questions.explain: Proteins (amino acids), nucleic acids (nucleotides), and polysaccharides (sugars) are polymers of monomers. Lipids are grouped by being hydrophobic; fats are made of glycerol plus fatty acids, not long chains of repeating units.

questions.q: Why are fats and fatty acid tails hydrophobic?
choices: They carry a strong positive charge that repels water.
They contain many –OH groups that repel water.
They are held together by ionic bonds that break in water.
They consist mostly of nonpolar C–H and C–C bonds, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
questions.explain: Hydrocarbon chains share electrons almost equally (C–H difference about 0.35), so they have no partial charges for water to attract. –OH groups would make a molecule more hydrophilic, not less.

questions.q: In a phospholipid bilayer, why do the fatty acid tails face inward and the phosphate heads face outward?
choices: The heads are hydrophobic and hide from water inside the bilayer.
The tails are attracted to water and reach toward the cytoplasm.
The hydrophobic tails avoid water by facing each other, while the hydrophilic heads interact with the water on both sides.
Covalent bonds between neighboring heads force the tails inward.
questions.explain: Because phospholipids are amphipathic, in water they arrange themselves so the polar heads touch the watery fluid inside and outside the cell, and the nonpolar tails are tucked away. The bilayer is held together by these hydrophobic effects, not by covalent bonds between lipids.

questions.q: Which is a main function of biological membranes, as described in class?
choices: Storing hereditary information
Catalyzing every chemical reaction in the cell
Providing rigid structural support like a cell wall
Acting as a barrier and regulating what enters and leaves
questions.explain: Membranes act as a selective barrier, regulate entry and exit, and provide surfaces where chemical reactions happen. DNA stores hereditary information, and rigid support comes from the cell wall.

questions.q: In the fluid mosaic model, which type of protein is noncovalently attached to the membrane surface, either to integral proteins or to phospholipid heads?
choices: Transmembrane protein
Peripheral membrane protein
Lipid-anchored protein
Integral membrane protein that crosses the bilayer
questions.explain: Peripheral proteins sit on the surface held by noncovalent interactions. Transmembrane proteins span the bilayer, and lipid-anchored proteins are covalently attached to a lipid inserted in the membrane; both of these are integral proteins.

questions.q: The membrane-spanning segments of most transmembrane proteins are alpha-helices made mostly of nonpolar amino acids. Why?
choices: Nonpolar amino acids form hydrogen bonds with the phosphate heads.
Polar amino acids are too large to fit in a helix.
Nonpolar amino acids carry charges that attract the fatty acid tails.
The nonpolar side chains interact favorably with the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.
questions.explain: The middle of the bilayer is made of hydrocarbon tails, so the protein segment buried there must also be hydrophobic. Nonpolar side chains are uncharged.

questions.q: How often does a phospholipid 'flip-flop' to the opposite leaflet compared with moving laterally?
choices: Flip-flop happens constantly, while lateral movement is rare.
Both happen equally often, with no energy required.
Lateral movement within a leaflet is frequent, but flip-flop is rare and normally requires an ATP-driven enzyme (flippase).
Neither happens; membrane lipids are fixed in place.
questions.explain: Moving the polar head through the hydrophobic core is energetically unfavorable, so flip-flop does not happen spontaneously and needs flippase plus ATP. Rotating and moving sideways within a leaflet happen easily and constantly, which is why the membrane is called fluid.

questions.q: Which change would make a membrane MORE fluid?
choices: Replacing saturated fatty acid tails with shorter, unsaturated tails
Replacing unsaturated tails with longer, saturated tails
Lowering the temperature
Removing all double bonds from the fatty acid tails
questions.explain: Shorter tails and more double bonds (kinks) reduce packing and interactions between tails, increasing fluidity. Longer, saturated tails and lower temperatures make membranes more rigid.

questions.q: Two artificial bilayers are made: X with saturated phospholipids and Y with kinked unsaturated phospholipids. Which better serves a cell that needs a low-fluidity barrier that keeps substances from easily passing through?
choices: Y, because kinks pack more tightly than straight tails
Y, because unsaturated tails are polar and block ions
They would be identical, because fluidity depends only on the heads
X, because straight saturated tails pack tightly, making the membrane less fluid and less permeable
questions.explain: Tight packing of straight saturated tails lowers fluidity and permeability. Kinks from double bonds open up gaps, increasing fluidity. Fatty acid tails are nonpolar whether they are saturated or not.

questions.q: How does cholesterol affect membrane fluidity at different temperatures?
choices: It always increases fluidity, regardless of temperature.
At high temperatures it stabilizes the membrane and reduces fluidity; at low temperatures it prevents phospholipids from clustering, which keeps the membrane from becoming too rigid.
It always decreases fluidity, regardless of temperature.
It has no effect, because it sits outside the bilayer.
questions.explain: Cholesterol is a two-way buffer of fluidity, embedded among the phospholipid tails. Answering 'always increases' or 'always decreases' misses the temperature-dependent role, which the study guide stresses.

questions.q: As the temperature of a membrane rises, what happens to phospholipid movement, and what would adding cholesterol do?
choices: Movement increases; adding cholesterol would restrain that movement and stabilize the membrane.
Movement decreases; cholesterol would increase it further.
Movement increases; cholesterol would make the membrane even more fluid.
Movement is unaffected by temperature; cholesterol would dissolve the membrane.
questions.explain: Heat gives lipids more kinetic energy, so fluidity rises. At higher temperatures cholesterol stabilizes the bilayer and raises its melting point, which counteracts excess fluidity.

questions.q: Which molecule crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer most easily?
choices: Na⁺
Glucose
O₂
An amino acid
questions.explain: Small, nonpolar gases like O₂ and CO₂ dissolve in the hydrophobic core and diffuse through readily. Ions are blocked by their charge, and large polar molecules such as glucose cross very slowly without transport proteins.

questions.q: Rank these from most to least permeable through a pure lipid bilayer: K⁺, CO₂, glucose.
choices: K⁺ > glucose > CO₂
Glucose > CO₂ > K⁺
CO₂ > glucose > K⁺
K⁺ > CO₂ > glucose
questions.explain: Permeability depends on size, polarity, and charge. Small nonpolar gases pass easily; large polar molecules like glucose pass very slowly; ions are the least permeable because charge is strongly excluded from the hydrophobic core.

questions.q: Why is the plasma membrane described as a 'fluid mosaic'?
choices: It is liquid water held in place by a protein mosaic.
Lipids and many proteins can move laterally within the membrane (fluid), and the membrane is a mix of different lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates (mosaic).
Its proteins are fixed in a rigid pattern, like tiles, that never moves.
It is made only of phospholipids arranged in a repeating pattern.
questions.explain: 'Fluid' refers to the lateral movement of components, and 'mosaic' to the varied pieces embedded in the bilayer. The proteins are not rigidly fixed.

questions.q: Which is NOT a type of function carried out by membrane proteins?
choices: Storing the cell's hereditary information
Transport
Acting as receptors for signals
Cell adhesion and recognition
questions.explain: Membrane proteins act as transporters, enzymes, receptors, and recognition and adhesion molecules. Hereditary information is stored in DNA.

questions.q: When phospholipids are mixed into water, they spontaneously form bilayer sheets or spheres rather than dissolving as single molecules. What is the main driving force?
choices: The hydrophobic effect: the nonpolar tails cluster away from water while the polar heads stay in contact with it
Covalent bonds forming between neighboring phospholipid heads
Ionic bonds between the fatty acid tails
ATP being used to assemble the bilayer
questions.explain: Bilayers (and micelles) self-assemble because hiding hydrophobic tails from water is energetically favorable. No covalent bonds or ATP are needed, which is why bilayers could form before the first cells existed.

questions.q: Which term means a substance dissolved in a fluid, and which means the fluid that dissolves it?
choices: Solvent is the dissolved substance; solute is the dissolving fluid.
Solute is the dissolved substance; solvent is the dissolving fluid.
Both terms mean the dissolved substance.
Solute is the membrane; solvent is the transport protein.
questions.explain: In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many polar and charged substances.

questions.q: What is a concentration gradient?
choices: The total amount of solvent in a cell
A protein that moves molecules across the membrane
A difference in the concentration of a substance between two neighboring regions
The speed at which a substance diffuses
questions.explain: A gradient is a physical difference (in concentration, charge, pressure, or temperature) between adjoining regions. Substances diffuse 'down' a concentration gradient, from high to low.

questions.q: In simple diffusion, which way do particles move?
choices: From high to low concentration (down their gradient), with no energy input from the cell
From low to high concentration, using ATP
Only through protein channels, using ATP
Only when the concentrations on both sides are equal
questions.explain: Simple diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient directly through the bilayer. Movement from low to high concentration requires energy, which is active transport.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and active transport?
choices: Simple and facilitated diffusion are both passive and move solutes down their gradient; only active transport uses energy to move solutes against their gradient.
Facilitated diffusion uses ATP because it needs a protein.
Simple diffusion moves solutes against their gradient.
All three move solutes from low to high concentration.
questions.explain: Facilitated diffusion uses channels or transporters but is still passive: the gradient drives it. Needing a protein does not mean needing energy, which is the most common misconception here.

questions.q: Glucose enters a cell through a carrier protein, moving from a high outside concentration to a low inside concentration, and no ATP is used. What kind of transport is this?
choices: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
questions.explain: A protein is involved, so it is not simple diffusion; the movement is down the gradient without energy, so it is not active transport. Transporters are the main route for uptake of sugars and amino acids.

questions.q: What is the difference between a channel and a transporter (carrier)?
choices: Channels always require ATP, while transporters never do.
Transporters form open pores, while channels change shape.
A channel forms an open passageway that solutes diffuse through, often gated; a transporter binds the solute and changes shape to move it across.
Channels move only water, while transporters move only ions.
questions.explain: Gated channels open (for example when a ligand binds) to let ions or molecules diffuse through. Transporters undergo a conformational change for each round of transport. Both can work passively.

questions.q: A transporter moves Na⁺ into the cell and glucose into the cell at the same time. What type of transporter is it?
choices: Uniporter
Antiporter
Gated channel
Symporter (cotransporter)
questions.explain: Symporters move two or more solutes in the same direction. Antiporters move them in opposite directions, and uniporters move a single solute.

questions.q: A transporter exchanges one H⁺ moving out of the cell for one Ca²⁺ moving in. What type of transporter is this?
choices: Antiporter
Symporter
Uniporter
Peripheral membrane protein
questions.explain: Two solutes moving in opposite directions defines an antiporter. A symporter would move them in the same direction.

questions.q: What distinguishes primary active transport from secondary active transport?
choices: Primary active transport is passive; secondary active transport uses ATP.
Secondary active transport moves only water.
Primary active transport uses energy directly, for example from ATP in a pump; secondary active transport uses an existing ion gradient to drive another solute against its gradient.
Primary active transport needs no protein; secondary active transport uses channels.
questions.explain: A pump such as the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses ATP directly. Symporters and antiporters can then harness the Na⁺ or H⁺ gradient that the pump created to move nutrients uphill. That is indirect use of energy.

questions.q: What does the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase do?
choices: Uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell, against their gradients
Lets Na⁺ and K⁺ diffuse freely down their gradients
Pumps 3 K⁺ out and 2 Na⁺ in without using energy
Makes ATP as Na⁺ flows into the cell
questions.explain: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is the classic primary active transporter: each cycle uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. The gradients it builds power neuronal signaling and secondary active transport.

questions.q: A drug blocks the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Over time, what happens to nutrient uptake by Na⁺-coupled symporters?
choices: It increases, because more Na⁺ stays outside the cell.
It decreases, because the Na⁺ gradient that powers the symporters runs down.
It is unaffected, because symporters do not need any energy source.
It increases, because symporters start using ATP directly.
questions.explain: Secondary active transport depends on the Na⁺ gradient that the pump maintains. Once the pump stops, Na⁺ leaks in, the gradient dissipates, and symport of nutrients against their gradient fails.

questions.q: A cell keeps an amino acid at 10 times higher concentration inside than outside. Which mechanism must it be using to bring in more of that amino acid?
choices: Simple diffusion, because amino acids are small
Facilitated diffusion through a channel
Active transport, because the amino acid must move against its concentration gradient
Osmosis
questions.explain: Moving a solute from low to high concentration requires energy, either directly (a pump) or indirectly (a coupled ion gradient). Passive mechanisms can only move it down its gradient.

questions.q: Which function is driven by an H⁺ electrochemical gradient, according to the lecture?
choices: Storing genetic information in the nucleus
Synthesizing ATP in mitochondria and chloroplasts
Forming peptide bonds on the ribosome
Making the phospholipid bilayer self-assemble
questions.explain: Ion gradients do a lot of work: H⁺ gradients power ATP synthesis and bacterial flagella, Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients power nerve signals, and Ca²⁺ gradients regulate muscle contraction.

questions.q: Which molecule would most likely need a transport protein to cross the plasma membrane at a useful rate?
choices: O₂
CO₂
A small nonpolar lipid-soluble molecule
Na⁺
questions.explain: Ions are charged and essentially cannot pass through the hydrophobic core without channels or transporters. Small nonpolar molecules and gases cross by simple diffusion.

questions.q: What is osmosis?
choices: The diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration
The diffusion of solute across a membrane from low to high solute concentration
The active pumping of water using ATP
The movement of any molecule through a protein channel
questions.explain: Osmosis is a special case of diffusion for water. Water moves down its own concentration gradient, which means it moves toward the side with more solute.

questions.q: Water moves by osmosis toward which side of a membrane?
choices: The side with the lower solute concentration
The side with more water already
The side with the higher solute concentration (lower water concentration)
The side with more ATP
questions.explain: More solute means relatively less free water, so water diffuses toward it. A common trap is to think water moves toward where there is 'more water'; it actually moves away from it.

questions.q: How are the terms hypertonic and hypotonic related?
choices: Hypertonic always means a 10% solution, and hypotonic means pure water.
They are relative: if solution A has more solute than solution B, A is hypertonic to B and B is hypotonic to A.
Hypertonic means having more water than the other solution.
A solution can be hypertonic only to itself.
questions.explain: Tonicity describes one solution compared with another. The solution with more solute is hypertonic, the one with less is hypotonic, and equal solute means isotonic.

questions.q: A red blood cell with an internal solute concentration of 6% is placed in a 17% salt solution. What happens?
choices: The solution is hypotonic, so water enters the cell and it bursts.
The solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cell and the cell shrinks.
The solution is isotonic, so there is no net water movement.
Salt rushes into the cell, and the cell swells.
questions.explain: 17% outside is more solute than 6% inside, so the outside is hypertonic and water moves out of the cell. Thinking the salt itself moves in ignores that the membrane largely blocks ions.

questions.q: The same red blood cells (6% internal solute) are placed in a 3% solution. What happens?
choices: Water moves out of the cells, which shrink, because the solution is hypertonic.
Water moves into the cells, which swell and may burst, because the solution is hypotonic.
Nothing changes, because 3% is close to 6%.
The cells actively pump water out using ATP to stay the same size.
questions.explain: Less solute outside means more water outside, so water enters by osmosis. Animal cells lack a cell wall, so they can swell until they lyse (osmotic burst).

questions.q: In which solution would a red blood cell with 6% internal solute show no net change in volume?
choices: A 3% solution
A 17% solution
A 6% solution
Pure distilled water
questions.explain: Equal solute concentration inside and outside (isotonic) means water moves in and out at equal rates, so there is no net movement and no change in volume.

questions.q: A shipwrecked sailor drinks seawater. Why does this make dehydration worse?
choices: Seawater makes blood hypotonic, so cells swell and burst.
Salt molecules carry water out of the body through the lungs.
Seawater has no effect on cells, because salt cannot affect osmosis.
Seawater raises blood salt concentration, making blood hypertonic to body cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.
questions.explain: When the extracellular fluid has more solute than the cells, water moves out of the cells into the salty fluid, dehydrating them even though water was swallowed.

questions.q: A U-tube is divided by a membrane permeable to water but not to solute. Side A holds a 2% solution and side B a 20% solution. What happens?
choices: Side B is hypotonic, so water moves from B to A.
Solute moves from B to A until both sides are 11%.
Side B is hypertonic, so water moves from A to B and the liquid level rises on side B.
Nothing happens, because the membrane blocks all movement.
questions.explain: Only water can cross, so water moves toward the higher solute concentration (B), increasing B's volume. Solute cannot cross, so the solute itself does not move to even things out.

questions.q: What is required for osmosis to cause a change in volume on either side of a membrane?
choices: The membrane must be permeable to both water and solute.
The membrane must be permeable to water but not to the solute, and the solute concentrations on the two sides must differ.
The cell must use ATP to push water across.
The solute concentrations must be equal on both sides.
questions.explain: If the solute could cross freely, it would diffuse to equalize concentrations and no net water shift would build up. If the concentrations are equal, the solution is isotonic and there is no net water flow.

questions.q: A red onion cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution, and its plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall. What is this called, and why does it happen?
choices: Lysis: the solution is hypotonic, so water enters and the cell bursts.
Turgor: the solution is hypotonic, so the vacuole swells against the wall.
Plasmolysis: the solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the central vacuole and cytoplasm by osmosis.
Plasmolysis: salt enters the cell and pushes the membrane away from the wall.
questions.explain: In a hypertonic solution plant cells lose water, the vacuole shrinks, and the membrane detaches from the rigid wall. Higher salt concentrations generally cause more cells to plasmolyze.

questions.q: Why does a plant cell in a hypotonic solution become firm (turgid) rather than bursting like a red blood cell?
choices: Plant cells have no aquaporins, so water cannot enter.
Water enters, but the rigid cell wall pushes back and prevents the cell from expanding until it ruptures.
Plant cells actively pump all incoming water back out.
Hypotonic solutions draw water out of plant cells.
questions.explain: Both cell types take in water in a hypotonic solution; the difference is that the wall resists expansion and creates turgor pressure. Animal cells have no wall, so they can lyse.

questions.q: Container A holds 5% salt solution and container B holds 15% salt solution. Which statement is correct?
choices: B has the higher concentration of water, so water would move from B into A.
Both have the same water concentration, because both are salt solutions.
A has the higher concentration of water, so if the containers were connected by a water-permeable membrane, water would move from A into B.
Water would move from A into B because A has more salt.
questions.explain: A 5% salt solution is 95% water, while 15% salt is 85% water. Water diffuses from higher water concentration (A) to lower water concentration (B), which is the same as moving toward more solute.

questions.q: In an onion cell experiment, 0% of cells plasmolyzed in 0.2 M NaCl, 60% in 0.4 M, and 100% in 0.8 M. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
choices: 0.2 M is close to isotonic for these cells, and solutions become increasingly hypertonic as the concentration rises.
0.2 M is strongly hypertonic, because it caused no plasmolysis.
0.8 M is hypotonic, so every cell gained water.
Plasmolysis is unrelated to salt concentration.
questions.explain: No plasmolysis means no net water loss, which fits a roughly isotonic solution. Rising salt makes the outside increasingly hypertonic, so more cells lose water and plasmolyze.

questions.q: Which statement about 'concentration' is correct?
choices: Concentration is the total volume of a solution, regardless of solute.
Adding more water increases the concentration of a solute.
Concentration only applies to gases, not to solutions.
Concentration is the amount of solute in a given amount of solvent, so adding solute to the same volume increases concentration.
questions.explain: Concentration expresses solute per amount of solvent. Diluting with water lowers solute concentration (and raises the concentration of water), which is how hypotonic solutions are made.

questions.q: What are the three components of a nucleotide?
choices: An amino group, a carboxyl group, and an R group
Glycerol, two fatty acids, and a phosphate group
A phosphate group, a five-carbon (pentose) sugar, and a nitrogenous base
A ribosome, a codon, and an amino acid
questions.explain: Nucleotides, the monomers of DNA and RNA, contain a phosphate, a pentose sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), and a base. An amino group, carboxyl group, and R group describe an amino acid.
