questions.q: Which bases are purines, and which are pyrimidines?
choices: Purines: cytosine and thymine; pyrimidines: adenine and guanine
Purines: adenine and thymine; pyrimidines: guanine and cytosine
All five bases are purines.
Purines (double ring): adenine and guanine; pyrimidines (single ring): cytosine, thymine, and uracil
questions.explain: The structural difference is ring number: purines have two fused rings, and pyrimidines have one. A memory aid is that the shorter word, pyrimidine, has the bigger, double-ring base.

questions.q: Which features distinguish an RNA nucleotide from a DNA nucleotide?
choices: RNA has deoxyribose and thymine; DNA has ribose and uracil.
RNA nucleotides lack a phosphate group.
DNA nucleotides contain amino acids, while RNA nucleotides do not.
RNA has ribose, with an –OH on the 2′ carbon, and can contain uracil; DNA has deoxyribose, with H on the 2′ carbon, and contains thymine.
questions.explain: 'Deoxy' means one oxygen is missing: deoxyribose has H instead of OH at the 2′ carbon. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA. Both still have a phosphate attached at the 5′ carbon.

questions.q: Which bonds hold the two strands of a DNA double helix together, and which bonds form each sugar-phosphate backbone?
choices: Hydrogen bonds between paired bases hold the strands together; covalent phosphodiester bonds form the backbone.
Phosphodiester bonds hold the strands together; hydrogen bonds form the backbone.
Ionic bonds hold the strands together; peptide bonds form the backbone.
Peptide bonds hold the strands together; ester bonds form the backbone.
questions.explain: Strong covalent phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within a strand. Weaker hydrogen bonds between complementary bases let the two strands separate for replication and transcription.

questions.q: In a DNA double helix, which parts face the interior and which face the exterior?
choices: The sugar-phosphate backbones face the interior; the bases face outward.
Phosphates face the interior; sugars and bases face outward.
Everything is randomly arranged.
The nitrogenous bases face the interior, paired with each other; the sugar-phosphate backbones are on the outside.
questions.explain: The hydrophilic, charged sugar-phosphate backbone faces the surrounding water, while the flatter, more hydrophobic bases stack and pair inside, like rungs of a twisted ladder.

questions.q: Two nitrogenous bases are joined by three hydrogen bonds. Which base pair is it?
choices: Adenine–thymine
Adenine–guanine
Cytosine–thymine
Guanine–cytosine
questions.explain: G pairs with C through three hydrogen bonds; A pairs with T through two. A–G and C–T are not complementary pairs, because each pair must be one purine plus one pyrimidine that fit together.

questions.q: A DNA sample is 20% thymine. According to Chargaff's rule, what are the percentages of the other bases?
questions.explain: In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C. With T = 20%, A = 20%, so A + T = 40% and G + C = 60%, split evenly as 30% each.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA sample is 35% guanine. What percentage is adenine?
questions.explain: G = C = 35% totals 70%, leaving 30% for A + T, and A = T = 15%. Answering 35% wrongly pairs A with G.

questions.q: What is the complementary strand of 5′-AACGTCGG-3′, written in the 5′ to 3′ direction?
choices: 5′-TTGCAGCC-3′
5′-CCGACGTT-3′
5′-UUGCAGCC-3′
5′-GGCTGCAA-3′
questions.explain: Pairing base by base gives 3′-TTGCAGCC-5′; reading that strand from its 5′ end gives 5′-CCGACGTT-3′. Writing TTGCAGCC with a 5′ label ignores that the strands are antiparallel. U belongs in RNA, and GGCTGCAA is just the original sequence written backward.

questions.q: What is the complement of 5′-GACCTTAG-3′?
choices: 5′-CTGGAATC-3′
3′-GACCTTAG-5′
3′-CUGGAAUC-5′
3′-CTGGAATC-5′
questions.explain: A pairs with T and G with C, and the strands are antiparallel, so the complement runs 3′ to 5′ beneath the original. Writing it 5′-CTGGAATC-3′ gets the bases right but the direction wrong, which reverses the meaning.

questions.q: In the DNA nucleotide numbering system, which carbon of the sugar is the base attached to, and which carbon is the phosphate attached to?
choices: The base is attached to the 5′ carbon; the phosphate to the 1′ carbon.
Both are attached to the 3′ carbon.
The base is attached to the 2′ carbon; the phosphate to the 3′ carbon.
The base is attached to the 1′ carbon; the phosphate is attached to the 5′ carbon.
questions.explain: Sugar carbons are numbered 1′ to 5′. The base is on 1′, the phosphate on 5′, and the 3′ –OH links to the next nucleotide's phosphate, which gives strands their 5′ to 3′ direction.

questions.q: In Griffith's experiment, mice injected with heat-killed smooth (S) bacteria mixed with live rough (R) bacteria died, and live S bacteria were recovered. What did this show?
choices: Heat brings dead bacteria back to life.
R bacteria are normally deadly to mice.
Proteins are definitely the genetic material.
Genetic material from the dead S cells transformed the R cells, giving them the capsule trait, which their offspring inherited.
questions.explain: Neither heat-killed S nor live R alone killed mice, so a 'transforming principle' must have passed from the dead S cells to the R cells. Griffith could not identify what it was; later work showed it was DNA.

questions.q: What happens chemically when nucleotides are joined into a DNA strand?
choices: A hydrolysis reaction adds a water molecule for each bond formed.
Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent sugars in the same strand.
Peptide bonds form between the bases.
A dehydration reaction removes a water molecule each time a nucleotide is added, forming a phosphodiester bond.
questions.explain: Polymers are built by dehydration (water removed) and broken down by hydrolysis (water added), and both are catalyzed by enzymes. Hydrogen bonds connect bases on opposite strands, not neighboring nucleotides in one strand.

questions.q: Arrange these levels of DNA organization from smallest to largest.
choices: Nucleotide → strand → double helix → chromosome → genome
Genome → chromosome → double helix → strand → nucleotide
Strand → nucleotide → chromosome → double helix → genome
Nucleotide → chromosome → strand → genome → double helix
questions.explain: Nucleotides polymerize into a strand, two strands form the double helix, DNA plus proteins forms a chromosome, and all the genetic material together is the genome.

questions.q: Why do many gene-regulatory proteins bind DNA in the major groove?
choices: The major groove is where the strands are covalently linked.
The major groove is wider, so proteins can contact the edges of the bases and recognize specific sequences.
The major groove contains no bases, only phosphates.
Proteins can only bind single-stranded DNA.
questions.explain: The grooves expose the edges of base pairs. The wider major groove gives proteins room to 'read' the sequence, which is how many proteins that affect gene expression find their binding sites.

questions.q: What is a nucleosome?
choices: A single histone protein with no DNA
A loop of RNA attached to a ribosome
A region of the nucleus where rRNA is made
About 146 to 147 bp of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histone proteins, the repeating unit of eukaryotic chromatin
questions.explain: Each nucleosome core has two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, with DNA wrapped around it; linker DNA connects nucleosomes. The region where rRNA is made is the nucleolus, which has a similar-sounding name.

questions.q: Which histone binds the linker DNA between nucleosomes and helps form the 30-nm fiber?
choices: H2A
H3
H1
H4
questions.explain: H1 sits on the linker region and, with other proteins, helps nucleosomes pack into the more compact 30-nm fiber. H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 form the octamer core.

questions.q: Why must eukaryotic DNA be wrapped around histones and further compacted?
choices: To keep DNA from forming hydrogen bonds between its strands.
To convert DNA into RNA.
Because DNA is too short to function without protein extensions.
A chromosome's DNA can be about a meter long but must fit into a nucleus within a cell only 10 to 100 µm across.
questions.explain: Wrapping into nucleosomes shortens DNA about 7-fold, the 30-nm fiber another 7-fold, and loop domains compact it further. Compaction also helps regulate which genes are accessible.

questions.q: How are loop domains formed in chromatin?
choices: Ribosomes pull the DNA into loops during translation.
CTCF proteins bound at specific sites pair with each other, and SMC proteins encircle two DNA segments, folding the 30-nm fiber into loops.
Histone H1 cuts the DNA into separate loops.
The nuclear envelope folds around each gene.
questions.explain: CTCF binds CCCTC repeats, and two CTCF molecules bind each other to close a loop; SMC dimers wrap two DNA segments together, often near CTCF sites.

questions.q: Can tightly condensed (closed) chromatin be readily transcribed?
choices: Yes. Condensed DNA is transcribed fastest because the genes are closer together.
No. Transcription is difficult or impossible because RNA polymerase and transcription factors cannot easily reach the DNA.
Yes, but only in prokaryotes.
No, because condensed chromatin has no DNA in it.
questions.explain: Gene expression needs access. In the closed conformation the DNA is packed with proteins; in the open conformation it is accessible. Condensed chromatin still contains DNA; the DNA is just not accessible.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts euchromatin with heterochromatin?
choices: Euchromatin is more compacted and silenced; heterochromatin is open and active.
Euchromatin is RNA; heterochromatin is DNA.
Euchromatin is less compacted and generally transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is highly compacted and generally silenced.
They differ only in their DNA sequence, not in compaction.
questions.explain: The difference is in packing, not sequence: the same DNA can be euchromatic in one cell and heterochromatic in another (facultative heterochromatin).

questions.q: What is the difference between facultative and constitutive heterochromatin?
choices: Facultative heterochromatin is found only in prokaryotes.
Constitutive heterochromatin is open in every cell type.
Facultative heterochromatin is located only at telomeres.
Facultative heterochromatin is compact and silenced in some cell types but open in others; constitutive heterochromatin is compact in all cell types, typically at centromeres and telomeres.
questions.explain: 'Constitutive' means always: those regions, such as centromeres and telomeres, are condensed everywhere. 'Facultative' means optional: the region is silenced in some cell types but active in others. Once formed in development, it is maintained through cell divisions.

questions.q: What does histone acetyltransferase (HAT) do, and how does it affect transcription?
choices: It removes acetyl groups from histones, condensing chromatin and repressing transcription.
It adds methyl groups to cytosine, silencing the gene.
It adds acetyl groups to histones, loosening their grip on DNA so chromatin opens and transcription increases.
It cuts DNA at the linker regions.
questions.explain: Acetylation neutralizes positive charges on histones, which reduces their attraction to negatively charged DNA and opens the chromatin. The reverse enzyme, histone deacetylase, condenses chromatin and represses genes.

questions.q: A drug inhibits histone deacetylase (HDAC). What would you predict for many genes in treated cells?
choices: Histones lose their acetyl groups, and transcription stops.
DNA becomes methylated, and genes are silenced.
Histones stay acetylated, chromatin stays more open, and transcription of those genes tends to increase.
Nucleosomes are converted into ribosomes.
questions.explain: HDAC normally removes acetyl groups to compact chromatin. Blocking it leaves acetyl groups on, so the chromatin is looser and more accessible. Methylation is done by a different enzyme, DNA methyltransferase.

questions.q: In DNA methylation in vertebrates, which nucleotide is methylated, and what is the usual effect?
choices: Adenine; methylation always activates transcription.
Cytosine, often in CpG sites near promoters; methylation usually inhibits transcription.
Guanine; methylation has no effect on genes.
Uracil; methylation converts DNA into RNA.
questions.explain: DNA methyltransferase adds methyl groups to cytosine. Methylated CpG islands are associated with repressed genes and unmethylated ones with active genes. Methylation can block activators or recruit repressing proteins.

questions.q: In many adults the lactase gene is turned off after weaning because a cytosine in an upstream enhancer becomes methylated. What chain of events explains the silencing?
choices: Methylation opens the chromatin, so too much lactase is made and is then degraded.
Methylation condenses the chromatin, so activator proteins cannot bind the enhancer, and little lactase is transcribed.
Methylation changes the lactase amino acid sequence.
Methylation removes the gene from the chromosome.
questions.explain: Methylated DNA is associated with condensed chromatin, which blocks activator binding to the enhancer, so transcription drops. The DNA sequence and protein sequence are unchanged; this is an epigenetic change.

questions.q: Some people carry a C → T mutation at the methylated site in the lactase enhancer and keep digesting milk as adults. Why?
choices: The mutation changes the lactase enzyme so it digests lactose faster.
Without that cytosine, the site cannot be methylated, so the enhancer stays open, activators bind, and the lactase gene stays on.
Thymine is methylated more strongly, which activates the gene.
The mutation deletes the enhancer, which turns the gene on.
questions.explain: DNA methylation targets cytosine. Replacing the C with T removes the target, so normal epigenetic silencing cannot happen, and the enhancer keeps supporting transcription. The mutation is in a regulatory region, not in the protein-coding sequence.

questions.q: What are nucleosome-free regions (NFRs)?
choices: Regions where DNA is wrapped twice as tightly around histones
Parts of RNA where ribosomes cannot bind
Regions of constitutive heterochromatin at the centromere
Stretches of about 150 bp, often at the start and end of genes, that lack nucleosomes and are flanked by the −1 and +1 nucleosomes
questions.explain: NFRs give transcription machinery access to DNA. They may be required for transcription, but they are not sufficient to activate a gene on their own.

questions.q: Which is one way ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling complexes can change chromatin?
choices: By adding amino acids to the histone tails using ribosomes
By shifting nucleosome positions, evicting histone octamers, or swapping standard histones for histone variants
By converting heterochromatin into RNA
By permanently deleting promoters
questions.explain: Remodeling complexes use ATP to reposition nucleosomes, remove them (creating gaps), or change their histone makeup, making DNA more or less accessible. Activators often recruit these complexes to promoters.

questions.q: What is the 'histone code' hypothesis?
choices: The DNA sequence that encodes the histone proteins.
The triplet code that converts mRNA into amino acids.
The idea that histones carry genetic information instead of DNA.
Patterns of histone modifications act like a code that is read by proteins, attracting either activators or repressors of transcription.
questions.explain: Specific combinations of modifications such as acetylation and methylation on histone tails recruit specific proteins, so one pattern promotes transcription while another inhibits it. It is not the genetic code.

questions.q: What are epigenetic alterations?
choices: Point mutations that change a single base pair
Heritable changes in gene expression that do not change the DNA sequence, such as DNA methylation and histone modifications
Changes in the amino acid sequence of a protein
Deletions of entire chromosomes
questions.explain: 'Epi-' means 'on top of': the marks sit on the DNA or histones and can be passed to daughter cells, but the sequence itself is unchanged. A base-pair change is a mutation, not an epigenetic change.

questions.q: What does the central dogma of molecular biology describe?
choices: The flow of information from protein to RNA to DNA
The process by which cells divide
The breakdown of glucose to make ATP
The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA (transcription) to protein (translation)
questions.explain: Genetic information in DNA is transcribed into RNA, and mRNA is translated into a polypeptide. Going backward from protein to nucleic acid does not happen.

questions.q: How does a gene relate to a chromosome?
choices: A gene is a specific region of DNA along a chromosome that carries the information for one protein or functional RNA.
A chromosome is a small piece of a gene.
Genes and chromosomes are two names for the same thing.
Genes are found in the cytoplasm, and chromosomes in the nucleus.
questions.explain: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule with its proteins, and it carries many genes. Each gene is a discrete region that usually encodes a single protein or RNA.

questions.q: Which match of the three major RNA classes with their functions is correct?
choices: mRNA catalyzes peptide bonds; tRNA forms the ribosome; rRNA carries the code.
mRNA brings amino acids; tRNA carries the code; rRNA is the template for DNA.
All three carry codons that specify amino acids.
mRNA carries the coding sequence to the ribosome; tRNA brings amino acids and reads codons; rRNA forms the ribosome and catalyzes peptide bonds.
questions.explain: Messenger RNA is the template for translation, transfer RNA adapts codons to amino acids, and ribosomal RNA is structural and catalytic (the ribosome is a ribozyme). Only mRNA carries the codons.

questions.q: What is reverse transcription?
choices: Copying DNA into RNA in the 3′ to 5′ direction
Translating a protein back into mRNA
Copying an RNA template into DNA (cDNA), as retroviruses do using reverse transcriptase
Removing introns from pre-mRNA
questions.explain: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, against the usual flow of the central dogma. DNA copied from a mature mRNA lacks introns, because they were already spliced out. Protein is never translated back into nucleic acid.

questions.q: What is a codon, and how many different codons are there?
choices: A sequence of three mRNA nucleotides; there are 64 possible codons.
A sequence of two nucleotides; there are 16 possible codons.
A single nucleotide; there are 4 possible codons.
A sequence of three amino acids; there are 20 possible codons.
questions.explain: With 4 bases read three at a time, there are 4³ = 64 combinations. 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons. Doublets would give only 16, which is too few for 20 amino acids.

questions.q: Why is the genetic code described as redundant (degenerate)?
choices: Each codon specifies several different amino acids.
Every gene is present in many copies.
Stop codons also code for amino acids.
Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, because 61 codons encode only 20 amino acids.
questions.explain: Redundancy means many codons code for the same amino acid. The reverse is not true: each codon specifies only one amino acid, which is why the code is also called unambiguous.

questions.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is nearly universal?
choices: Every organism has exactly the same genes.
All proteins contain all 20 amino acids.
Almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids, which is why a human gene can be expressed in bacteria.
The code changes randomly from cell to cell.
questions.explain: The shared code is strong evidence of common ancestry and is the basis of biotechnology. Sharing the code does not mean sharing the same genes.

questions.q: The genetic code is called 'conservative' because codons for the same amino acid often differ only in the third position. What is a consequence?
choices: Every mutation changes the protein dramatically.
The third base is never read by the ribosome.
Only the third base determines the amino acid.
Many single-base changes at the third position do not change the amino acid, which reduces the impact of mutations.
questions.explain: For example, GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG all code for glycine, so a change at the third base is often 'silent.' The ribosome still reads all three bases; it is the code's layout that buffers the change.

questions.q: Which amino acid begins nearly every newly made protein, and what is its codon?
choices: Methionine, UAA
Methionine, AUG
Glycine, GGG
Tryptophan, UGG
questions.explain: AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine, which sets the reading frame. UAA is a stop codon, and UGG codes for tryptophan.

questions.q: What is the role of the stop codons UAA, UAG, and UGA?
choices: They code for methionine and start translation.
They mark where introns begin.
They code for the three most common amino acids.
They signal the end of translation; no tRNA carries an amino acid for them, and release factors bind instead.
questions.explain: When a stop codon enters the A site, a release factor binds and the finished polypeptide is released. They are not where introns begin; introns are removed before the mRNA ever reaches the ribosome.

questions.q: Using the standard genetic code, which amino acid does the mRNA codon 5′-UGG-3′ specify?
choices: A stop signal
Tryptophan
Cysteine
Glycine
questions.explain: UGG is the only codon for tryptophan. UGA (one base different) is a stop codon, and UGU and UGC code for cysteine, which is why reading the third base carefully matters.

questions.q: How many amino acids are in the polypeptide encoded by the mRNA 5′-AUG UUU GGC AAA UAG-3′?
questions.explain: AUG (Met), UUU (Phe), GGC (Gly), AAA (Lys), then UAG is a stop codon, which adds no amino acid. Counting the stop codon gives the tempting answer of 5.

questions.q: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-AAG-5′. Which amino acid does it carry?
choices: Lysine (codon 5′-AAG-3′)
Leucine (codon 5′-CUU-3′)
Glutamic acid (codon 5′-GAA-3′)
Phenylalanine (codon 5′-UUC-3′)
questions.explain: The anticodon pairs antiparallel with the codon: 3′-AAG-5′ pairs with 5′-UUC-3′, which codes for phenylalanine. Reading the anticodon itself as the codon gives lysine, the most common mistake.

questions.q: A single extra nucleotide is inserted just after the start codon of a gene. What is the most likely effect on the protein?
choices: Only one amino acid is added, and the rest of the protein is normal.
There is no effect, because the code is redundant.
The start codon moves, but the protein is unchanged.
Every codon downstream is shifted, so the amino acid sequence after the insertion is changed (a frameshift), often reaching an early stop codon.
questions.explain: Codons are read in consecutive triplets from the start codon, so adding one base changes the grouping of everything after it. Redundancy protects only against some single-base substitutions, not insertions.

questions.q: A mutation changes an mRNA codon from GGU to GGC. What happens to the protein?
choices: Glycine is replaced by a stop codon.
The reading frame shifts.
Nothing changes, because both codons specify glycine.
Glycine is replaced by cysteine.
questions.explain: Both are glycine codons, so this is a silent change, which shows the redundancy of the code. A substitution does not shift the reading frame; only insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three do.

questions.q: What is transcription?
choices: The synthesis of a protein from an mRNA template
The copying of an entire chromosome before cell division
The removal of introns from pre-mRNA
The synthesis of an RNA copy of a gene using one DNA strand as a template
questions.explain: Transcription makes RNA from DNA. Translation makes protein from mRNA, replication copies DNA, and splicing removes introns.

questions.q: Where do transcription and translation occur in a eukaryotic cell?
choices: Both occur in the nucleus.
Transcription occurs in the nucleus; translation occurs in the cytoplasm on ribosomes.
Transcription occurs in the cytoplasm; translation occurs in the nucleus.
Both occur inside the Golgi apparatus.
questions.explain: In eukaryotes, mRNA is made and processed in the nucleus, then exported to the cytosol for translation. In bacteria, which have no nucleus, both happen in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: What is the template strand of DNA?
choices: The DNA strand that RNA polymerase reads to build a complementary RNA
The strand whose sequence is identical to the mRNA
The strand that is translated into protein
Both strands, which are always copied at the same time
questions.explain: The template strand is read 3′ to 5′, and the RNA is complementary to it. The opposite strand, the coding strand, matches the mRNA sequence except that it has T where the RNA has U.

questions.q: In which direction is RNA synthesized, and in which direction is the template read?
choices: RNA is made 5′ to 3′; the template strand is read 3′ to 5′.
RNA is made 3′ to 5′; the template is read 5′ to 3′.
Both run 5′ to 3′.
It differs randomly from gene to gene.
questions.explain: RNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3′ end of the growing chain, so RNA grows 5′ to 3′ while moving along an antiparallel template. Which DNA strand serves as template varies between genes, but this direction rule never changes.

questions.q: A DNA template strand reads 3′-CGTACCTAG-5′. What RNA is transcribed?
choices: 5′-GCATGGATC-3′
5′-GCAUGGAUC-3′
5′-CGUACCUAG-3′
5′-CUAGGUACG-3′
questions.explain: Pair each template base (C→G, G→C, T→A, A→U) and keep the RNA antiparallel, giving 5′-GCAUGGAUC-3′. The version with T is DNA, not RNA; CGUACCUAG just swaps T for U in the template without pairing; and CUAGGUACG has the right bases written in the wrong direction.

questions.q: The coding strand of a gene reads 5′-ATGGCTTAC-3′. What is the mRNA sequence?
choices: 5′-UACCGAAUG-3′
3′-UACCGAAUG-5′
5′-AUGGCUUAC-3′
5′-ATGGCTTAC-3′
questions.explain: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding (non-template) strand, with U in place of T. The complementary sequence would come from treating the coding strand as the template, which is a common mix-up.

questions.q: What are the roles of the promoter and the terminator in a gene?
choices: The promoter is translated into the first amino acids; the terminator becomes the stop codon.
The promoter removes introns; the terminator adds the poly-A tail.
Both are sequences inside the mature mRNA that bind ribosomes.
The promoter is where RNA polymerase (with its factors) binds and transcription begins; the terminator signals where transcription ends.
questions.explain: These are DNA control sequences: the promoter controls when and where transcription starts, and the terminator specifies its end. Neither is translated into protein.

questions.q: What are the three stages of transcription, in order?
choices: Initiation, elongation, termination
Elongation, initiation, termination
Capping, splicing, tailing
Initiation, translocation, release
questions.explain: In initiation, RNA polymerase recognizes the promoter and opens the DNA. In elongation, it builds RNA 5′ to 3′. In termination, it reaches the terminator and releases the transcript. Capping, splicing, and tailing are RNA processing steps.

questions.q: During transcription, which enzyme separates the DNA strands to form the open complex and synthesizes the RNA?
choices: DNA ligase
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
RNA polymerase
Reverse transcriptase
questions.explain: RNA polymerase recognizes the promoter, unwinds the DNA to form an open complex, and links ribonucleotides. Behind it, the DNA rewinds into a double helix.

questions.q: What happens during the elongation stage of transcription?
choices: Ribosomes join amino acids with peptide bonds.
RNA polymerase moves along the template, adding complementary ribonucleotides to the 3′ end of the growing RNA, while the DNA rewinds behind it.
RNA polymerase first recognizes the promoter.
The transcript and polymerase detach from the DNA.
questions.explain: Elongation is the RNA-building step. Promoter recognition belongs to initiation, release belongs to termination, and peptide bonds belong to translation.

questions.q: A mutation destroys the promoter of a gene. What is the most likely result?
choices: The mRNA is made but is never spliced.
RNA polymerase cannot bind and start properly, so little or no mRNA is made from that gene.
The protein is made with a different first amino acid.
Transcription continues past the end of the gene.
questions.explain: The promoter is needed for RNA polymerase to recognize where to start, so initiation fails. Running past the end of the gene would come from a terminator defect.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts transcription in bacteria and eukaryotes?
choices: Bacteria transcribe in the nucleus, while eukaryotes transcribe in the cytoplasm.
Eukaryotic mRNAs are translated immediately, without processing.
Only bacteria use promoters and terminators.
Eukaryotic RNA polymerase II needs general transcription factors at the promoter, and the pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus; bacterial mRNA can be translated right away.
questions.explain: Both use promoters and terminators, but eukaryotic promoters (such as those with a TATA box) are recognized with the help of GTFs, and eukaryotic transcripts are capped, tailed, and spliced before export. Bacteria have no nucleus.

questions.q: The DNA coding strand is 5′-TTGACA-3′. Which statement is correct?
choices: The template strand is 5′-TTGACA-3′, and the mRNA is 5′-AACUGU-3′.
The mRNA is 5′-TTGACA-3′, because mRNA keeps thymine.
The template strand is 3′-UUGACA-5′.
The template strand is 3′-AACTGT-5′, and the mRNA is 5′-UUGACA-3′.
questions.explain: The template is complementary to the coding strand, and the mRNA is complementary to the template, so the mRNA equals the coding strand with U instead of T. DNA never contains U.

questions.q: What are introns and exons?
choices: Exons are removed by splicing; introns are kept and translated.
Introns are DNA sequences that are never transcribed.
Exons are the 5′ cap and poly-A tail.
Introns are transcribed but removed by splicing; exons are kept in the mature mRNA and carry the coding sequence.
questions.explain: Both are present in pre-mRNA; splicing cuts out introns and joins exons. A helpful memory aid: exons are expressed, introns are 'in the way.'

questions.q: What is added to the 5′ end of a eukaryotic pre-mRNA during processing?
choices: A poly-A tail of 100 to 200 adenines
A TATA box
An anticodon
A 7-methylguanosine cap
questions.explain: Capping adds a modified guanine to the 5′ end. The poly-A tail goes on the 3′ end, and the TATA box is a DNA sequence in the promoter.

questions.q: What are the functions of the 5′ cap?
choices: It is needed for mRNA export from the nucleus and binding to the ribosome, and it helps protect the mRNA from degradation.
It marks where transcription should stop.
It codes for the first amino acid.
It removes introns from the pre-mRNA.
questions.explain: Ribosomes recognize the cap to start translation, and the cap also stabilizes the mRNA. It is added after transcription begins and is not translated.

questions.q: A eukaryotic mRNA is made without a 5′ cap. What would you predict?
choices: It would be poorly exported, degraded quickly, and inefficiently bound by ribosomes, so little protein would be made.
It would be translated faster because nothing blocks the ribosome.
It would be read in a different reading frame.
It would be transcribed again automatically.
questions.explain: Without the cap, the mRNA lacks the signal for export and ribosome binding and is unprotected from degradation, so protein output falls sharply.

questions.q: What is the role of the poly-A tail?
choices: It is translated into a string of lysines at the end of every protein.
It is encoded by a long stretch of T's at the end of each gene.
It increases mRNA stability and lifespan in the cytosol and helps export the mRNA from the nucleus.
It forms the anticodon loop of tRNA.
questions.explain: 100 to 200 adenines are added to the 3′ end after transcription. The tail is not encoded in the gene sequence and is not translated as part of the protein.

questions.q: Which statement about RNA processing in bacteria versus eukaryotes is correct?
choices: Bacterial mRNAs require more processing than eukaryotic mRNAs.
Both bacteria and eukaryotes splice most of their genes.
Bacterial mRNAs can be translated immediately, while eukaryotic pre-mRNAs must be capped, tailed, and spliced before leaving the nucleus.
Eukaryotic mRNAs are translated inside the nucleus while being spliced.
questions.explain: In bacteria transcription and translation can be coupled because there is no nucleus, and splicing is essentially absent (0% alternative splicing in E. coli). Eukaryotic mRNAs leave the nucleus only after processing.

questions.q: A pre-mRNA has the structure: exon 1, intron A, exon 2, intron B, exon 3. After normal splicing, what does the mature mRNA contain, between the cap and the tail?
choices: Exon 1 – exon 2 – exon 3
Intron A – intron B
Exon 1 – intron A – exon 2 – intron B – exon 3
Exon 3 – exon 2 – exon 1
questions.explain: Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons in their original linear order. The order of exons is not reversed.

questions.q: What is alternative splicing?
choices: Splicing introns into the mRNA instead of removing them
Adding a different cap to each mRNA
Producing different mature mRNAs from the same pre-mRNA by including or excluding certain exons
Translating one mRNA in all three reading frames
questions.explain: Splicing factors change which exon boundaries the spliceosome recognizes, so one gene can yield several protein isoforms, such as the α-tropomyosin variants. The linear order of the exons that are kept is maintained.

questions.q: What is the main evolutionary advantage of alternative splicing?
choices: It lets one gene encode several related polypeptides, enlarging the proteome without enlarging the genome.
It removes the need for promoters.
It prevents all mutations.
It allows proteins to be made without ribosomes.
questions.explain: Complex organisms get more protein diversity from a similar number of genes. Humans have about 22,000 genes, yet about 70% of them are alternatively spliced.

questions.q: Based on data presented in class, which organism would you expect to have the highest percentage of alternatively spliced genes?
choices: Homo sapiens (humans)
Escherichia coli (a bacterium)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast)
Caenorhabditis elegans (a small worm)
questions.explain: Alternative splicing increases with biological complexity: about 0% in E. coli, under 1% in yeast, about 2% in C. elegans, and about 70% in humans.

questions.q: Which statement about alternative splicing is FALSE?
choices: Some exons may be left out of the final mRNA.
It never changes the final mRNA product.
It can produce protein isoforms from one gene.
It is regulated by splicing factors.
questions.explain: The whole point of alternative splicing is to change which exons end up in the mature mRNA, which produces different isoforms. The other statements are true.

questions.q: A mutation destroys the signal that marks the boundary of an intron, so that intron is no longer removed. What would you predict?
choices: The intron sequence stays in the mRNA and is read as codons, which usually changes the protein or introduces an early stop codon.
The intron is translated but then cut out of the protein.
The mRNA becomes more stable and makes more normal protein.
Nothing changes, because introns are never translated under any condition.
questions.explain: Introns are normally removed before translation. If one is retained, the ribosome reads it like any other sequence, often changing the reading frame or hitting a stop codon. Proteins are not trimmed of intron sequences afterward.

questions.q: Is the poly-A tail encoded in the DNA sequence of the gene?
choices: No. It is added to the 3′ end of the pre-mRNA after transcription.
Yes. It is transcribed from a run of T's in the template strand.
Yes. It is part of the promoter sequence.
No. It is added to the 5′ end of the DNA.
questions.explain: Polyadenylation is a processing step: enzymes add adenines without a template. That is why the slides say the tail is not encoded in the gene sequence.

questions.q: What is translation?
choices: The synthesis of RNA using a DNA template
The synthesis of a polypeptide using the codon sequence of an mRNA, carried out by ribosomes
The processing of pre-mRNA into mature mRNA
The replication of DNA before cell division
questions.explain: Translation converts the nucleotide 'language' of mRNA into the amino acid 'language' of proteins. Making RNA from DNA is transcription.

questions.q: What are the three stages of translation?
choices: Capping, splicing, tailing
Transcription, processing, export
Initiation, elongation, termination
Recognition, open complex, rewinding
questions.explain: Translation uses the same three stage names as transcription, but the events are different. Capping, splicing, and tailing are mRNA processing.

questions.q: What are the roles of the ribosome's A, P, and E sites?
choices: The A site accepts the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA, the P site holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide, and the E site is where the empty tRNA exits.
The A site releases empty tRNAs, the P site accepts new tRNAs, and the E site forms peptide bonds.
All three sites bind mRNA codons with no tRNA involved.
The A site holds the start codon permanently, and the E site holds the stop codon.
questions.explain: A = aminoacyl, P = peptidyl, E = exit. During each elongation cycle, tRNAs move A → P → E as the ribosome shifts along the mRNA.

questions.q: During initiation of translation, which events occur?
choices: A release factor binds the stop codon and the subunits separate.
RNA polymerase binds the promoter and opens the DNA.
The small subunit binds the mRNA, the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with the AUG start codon, and the large subunit joins.
Peptidyl transfer moves the chain to the A-site tRNA.
questions.explain: Initiation assembles the complete ribosome at the start codon, with Met-tRNA in the P site. Release factors belong to termination, and RNA polymerase belongs to transcription.

questions.q: What happens during the peptidyl transfer step of elongation?
choices: The amino acid in the A site is transferred to the tRNA in the E site.
The mRNA is transferred from the small subunit to the large subunit.
The growing polypeptide is transferred from the tRNA in the P site to the amino acid on the tRNA in the A site, forming a new peptide bond.
A release factor transfers the polypeptide to the E site.
questions.explain: The new peptide bond forms between the chain and the incoming amino acid, so the A-site tRNA now holds the whole chain. Translocation then moves that tRNA to the P site.

questions.q: What catalyzes peptide bond formation in the ribosome?
choices: rRNA in the large subunit; the ribosome is a ribozyme
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
RNA polymerase
The mRNA itself
questions.explain: The catalytic site of the large subunit is made of RNA, so the ribosome is a ribozyme (a catalytic RNA). Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNAs; it does not join amino acids to each other.

questions.q: What does aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase do?
choices: It forms peptide bonds between amino acids on the ribosome.
It adds the 5′ cap to mRNA.
It reads the template strand during transcription.
It attaches the correct amino acid to its matching tRNA; there is one for each of the 20 amino acids.
questions.explain: Charging each tRNA with the right amino acid is what links the genetic code to protein sequence. Peptide bonds are formed by rRNA in the ribosome.

questions.q: Which structural features do all tRNAs share?
choices: A cloverleaf shape with an anticodon on one loop and an acceptor stem where the amino acid attaches
A 5′ cap and a poly-A tail
A double helix with a sugar-phosphate backbone on the inside
A TATA box and a terminator
questions.explain: The anticodon base-pairs with an mRNA codon, and the acceptor stem carries the amino acid. Caps and tails are features of mRNA.

questions.q: What triggers the termination of translation?
choices: A tRNA carrying a 'stop' amino acid binds the stop codon.
The ribosome reaches the poly-A tail and falls off.
RNA polymerase reaches the terminator sequence.
A stop codon enters the A site, a release factor binds, and the bond between the tRNA and the polypeptide is hydrolyzed, releasing the protein.
questions.explain: No tRNA recognizes stop codons; release factor proteins do. After release, the uncharged tRNAs leave and the ribosomal subunits separate. A terminator ends transcription, not translation.

questions.q: During elongation, a tRNA has just moved from the A site to the P site. What happens next?
choices: The tRNA in the P site immediately returns to the A site.
A new aminoacyl-tRNA whose anticodon matches the next codon enters the empty A site.
The ribosome subunits separate.
The mRNA is spliced to remove the codon just read.
questions.explain: After translocation the A site is open, so the next charged tRNA can enter. The cycle (entry, peptide bond, translocation) repeats until a stop codon arrives.

questions.q: A drug blocks translocation, the movement of the ribosome along the mRNA. What is the most direct effect?
choices: Elongation stalls after a peptide bond forms, because tRNAs cannot shift and the A site never reopens.
Transcription of all genes stops.
tRNAs can no longer be charged with amino acids.
The 5′ cap is removed from the mRNA.
questions.explain: Translocation moves the tRNAs from A to P to E and exposes the next codon. Without it, no new aminoacyl-tRNA can enter, so the chain stops growing. Charging and transcription are separate processes.

questions.q: An mRNA reads 5′-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3′. What polypeptide is made?
choices: Met–Phe–Gly–Stop–Lys
Met–Phe–Gly
Tyr–Lys–Pro
Phe–Gly–Met
questions.explain: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, and UAA = stop, so the chain is released after Gly. Tyr–Lys–Pro comes from translating the complementary (anticodon) sequence instead of the mRNA codons.

questions.q: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACCGTAGCATT-5′. What polypeptide is produced?
choices: Tyr–Arg–Ser–Ile
Met–Ala–Ser–Ile
Met–Arg–Ser
Met–Ala–Ser
questions.explain: Transcribe first: 5′-AUG GCA UCG UAA-3′. AUG = Met, GCA = Ala, UCG = Ser, and UAA = stop. Translating the DNA letters directly, without transcribing, gives the wrong amino acids.

questions.q: Why does each tRNA carry only one specific amino acid, and why does that matter?
choices: The mRNA chemically attaches the amino acid to the tRNA.
The ribosome checks each amino acid's R group against the codon.
Each aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase recognizes a particular tRNA and its amino acid, so the anticodon reliably delivers the amino acid the codon calls for.
tRNAs carry all 20 amino acids and release the correct one at the A site.
questions.explain: Accurate pairing between codon and anticodon is useful only if each tRNA was charged correctly. That is the job of the synthetases. The ribosome checks codon-anticodon pairing, not the amino acid.

questions.q: What is a polyribosome?
choices: A ribosome with several large subunits
A tRNA carrying several amino acids
A nucleolus that makes multiple rRNAs
Several ribosomes translating the same mRNA at the same time, each making its own copy of the polypeptide
questions.explain: Many ribosomes can move along one mRNA one after another, which greatly increases how much protein is made from a single transcript.

questions.q: What is gene expression?
choices: The copying of DNA before cell division
The physical appearance of a chromosome
The process by which the information in a gene is used to make a functional product, such as a protein or RNA
The rate at which a cell divides
questions.explain: Gene expression covers transcription, processing, and translation of a gene into a functional product. Most genes are regulated so their products are made at the right time and in the right amount, which saves energy.

questions.q: What is the difference between constitutive genes and regulated (inducible) genes?
choices: Constitutive genes are never expressed; inducible genes are always on.
Constitutive genes are expressed at fairly constant levels in all conditions; inducible genes are turned on or up only when needed.
Constitutive genes are found only in bacteria.
Inducible genes are expressed only in dead cells.
questions.explain: Housekeeping (constitutive) genes are needed all the time. Inducible genes respond to signals or conditions, so the cell makes those products only when it needs them.

questions.q: Muscle cells and nerve cells in the same person have the same genome. Why do they make different proteins?
choices: Each cell type has lost the genes it does not use.
Muscle cells have more chromosomes than nerve cells.
Gene regulation causes each differentiated cell type to express a different subset of genes and amounts of proteins.
Proteins are inherited directly, not made from genes.
questions.explain: Cell differentiation comes from differential gene expression: the same DNA, but different proteomes. Most specialized cells keep their full genome.

questions.q: Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin, and the genes switch during development. What does this illustrate?
choices: Mutation: the fetal gene mutates into the adult gene at birth.
Alternative splicing of the same hemoglobin exon.
Post-translational destruction of all hemoglobin at birth.
Developmental gene regulation: different genes are expressed at different life stages to match changing needs.
questions.explain: The fetus must pull oxygen from maternal blood, so it expresses a hemoglobin with higher oxygen affinity, and the genes switch later in development. No DNA change is involved.

questions.q: At which levels can eukaryotic gene expression be regulated?
choices: Transcription, RNA modification (processing), translation, and post-translation
Only at transcription
Only at DNA replication
Only after the protein is degraded
questions.explain: Eukaryotes regulate at many steps, with transcriptional control the most common. Bacteria rely mostly on transcriptional control.

questions.q: What is combinatorial control?
choices: The expression of a gene depends on the combined action of many factors, including activators, repressors, modulators, chromatin structure, and DNA methylation.
Each gene is controlled by exactly one protein.
Several genes combine into one mRNA.
Codons combine to specify a single amino acid.
questions.explain: The five factors from class are activators, repressors, small-molecule or protein modulation, chromatin changes, and DNA methylation. Together they set a gene's expression level.

questions.q: What is the TATA box, and what does it do?
choices: A sequence in mRNA where ribosomes bind
A sequence like 5′-TATAAAA-3′ about 25 bp upstream of the transcriptional start site that sets the precise starting point of transcription
The stop signal at the end of a gene
A sequence inside introns that is removed by splicing
questions.explain: The TATA box and the transcriptional start site form the core promoter. On its own, the core promoter supports only low, basal transcription.

questions.q: Which three features are found in most eukaryotic promoters?
choices: A start codon, a stop codon, and a poly-A tail
A 5′ cap, introns, and exons
An A site, a P site, and an E site
A TATA box, a transcriptional start site, and regulatory (response) elements
questions.explain: The core promoter (TATA box plus start site) positions RNA polymerase, and regulatory elements such as enhancers and silencers bind proteins that raise or lower transcription.

questions.q: How do enhancers and silencers differ?
choices: Enhancers are always inside exons; silencers are always inside introns.
Enhancers bind activators to increase transcription; silencers bind repressors to prevent transcription when the gene is not needed.
Enhancers stop transcription; silencers start it.
Both are found only in mature mRNA.
questions.explain: Both are DNA regulatory elements, often 50 to 100 bp upstream, but they can be far away (even 100,000 bp), downstream, or within introns.

questions.q: A repressor protein binds a silencer near a gene. What is the expected result?
choices: Transcription of the gene increases.
Transcription of that gene is reduced or blocked.
The gene's mRNA is spliced differently.
The protein is tagged with ubiquitin.
questions.explain: Repressors acting through silencers inhibit RNA polymerase from starting transcription, often through the mediator complex. Ubiquitin tagging is post-translational control.

questions.q: Which three components are required for regulated transcription of eukaryotic protein-coding genes?
choices: DNA polymerase, ligase, and helicase
Ribosomes, tRNA, and release factors
Histone deacetylase, ubiquitin, and proteasomes
RNA polymerase II, general transcription factors (GTFs), and the mediator complex
questions.explain: GTFs and RNA polymerase II assemble at the TATA box as the preinitiation complex, and mediator relays signals from activators and repressors to control the rate of initiation.

questions.q: What is the role of the mediator complex?
choices: It partially wraps around the GTFs and RNA polymerase II and passes signals from activators or repressors bound at enhancers or silencers, controlling how fast transcription begins.
It binds the TATA box and synthesizes RNA.
It removes introns from pre-mRNA.
It attaches amino acids to tRNA.
questions.explain: Mediator is the bridge between regulatory proteins and the basal machinery. It does not make RNA itself; RNA polymerase II does.

questions.q: Why does the DNA often form a loop when an activator bound to a distant enhancer stimulates transcription?
choices: Looping cuts the gene out of the chromosome.
Looping converts the enhancer into an intron.
Looping lets the ribosome translate the DNA directly.
Looping brings the activator on the enhancer into contact with mediator and the RNA polymerase complex at the promoter.
questions.explain: Enhancers can be thousands of bases away, and bending the DNA lets the bound activator physically interact with mediator and the preinitiation complex.

questions.q: What is the preinitiation complex?
choices: The assembly of general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II at the TATA box before transcription starts
The ribosome bound to the start codon
A cluster of histones that blocks the promoter
The spliceosome bound to an intron
questions.explain: Transcription cannot begin until the GTFs and RNA polymerase II come together at the core promoter. The ribosome at the start codon is translation initiation.

questions.q: Which is an example of post-translational control?
choices: Methylating DNA in the promoter
Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA
Activating a protein by phosphorylation, or tagging it with ubiquitin so a proteasome destroys it
Binding of an activator to an enhancer
questions.explain: Post-translational control acts on finished proteins, through phosphorylation by kinases, added carbohydrates, cleavage, or ubiquitin-tagged destruction, and lets the cell respond rapidly. DNA methylation and enhancer binding act at transcription, and splicing at RNA processing.

questions.q: A cell keeps an inactive enzyme in storage and activates it within seconds when conditions change. Why might this be better than turning on the enzyme's gene?
choices: Activating a gene is faster than modifying a protein.
Stored enzymes do not need to be folded.
Turning on genes requires a ribozyme.
Post-translational activation is much faster, because transcription and translation take time.
questions.explain: Regulation after transcription and translation lets cells respond quickly, while making a new protein from scratch requires transcription, processing, and translation first.

questions.q: Lactase is made only by certain cells lining the small intestine. Which is the best explanation for why other cells, such as skin cells, do not make it, even though they carry the lactase gene?
choices: In other cell types, the gene's regulatory regions are not bound by the needed activators and its chromatin is kept closed.
Skin cells have deleted the lactase gene.
Skin cells cannot carry out transcription.
The lactase protein is made in skin but immediately splices itself out.
questions.explain: All cells have the same genome; cell-type-specific activators and chromatin states determine where a gene is expressed. Deleting genes is not how cells specialize.

questions.q: What is the general structure shared by all amino acids?
choices: A central carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group (side chain)
A five-carbon sugar bonded to a phosphate and a base
Glycerol bonded to three fatty acids
Four fused carbon rings with an –OH group
questions.explain: All 20 amino acids share this backbone; only the R group differs, and it determines each amino acid's chemistry. A sugar, phosphate, and base make a nucleotide.

questions.q: How many different amino acids are commonly used to build proteins?
questions.explain: Cells use 20 amino acids. 4 is the number of bases, 64 the number of codons, and 61 the number of codons that specify amino acids.

questions.q: What determines whether an amino acid is classified as nonpolar, polar uncharged, or charged?
choices: Whether it has an amino group
Whether it has a carboxyl group
Its position in the polypeptide chain
The chemical properties of its R group (side chain)
questions.explain: Every amino acid has the same amino and carboxyl groups. Hydrocarbon R groups make it nonpolar, groups like –OH make it polar, and groups that gain or lose H⁺ make it charged.

questions.q: In a water-soluble protein, where would you expect most nonpolar amino acids to be located?
choices: On the outer surface, in contact with water
Buried in the interior of the folded protein, away from water
Only at the two ends of the chain
Randomly distributed, because R groups do not affect folding
questions.explain: Hydrophobic effects drive nonpolar side chains to cluster inside, while polar and charged side chains face the watery surroundings. In membrane proteins, nonpolar residues face the lipid tails instead.

questions.q: How is a peptide bond formed?
choices: By hydrolysis, which adds water between two R groups
By hydrogen bonding between two amino groups
By an ionic bond between two carboxyl groups
By a dehydration (condensation) reaction between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water
questions.explain: The carboxyl carbon bonds covalently to the amino nitrogen and one H₂O is released. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, which breaks peptide bonds.

questions.q: A protein is digested into its individual amino acids. What type of reaction is this, and what is consumed?
choices: Dehydration synthesis; water is released.
Hydrolysis; one water molecule is used for each peptide bond broken.
Denaturation; ATP is consumed.
Condensation; amino groups are released.
questions.explain: Breaking a polymer into monomers adds water across each bond (hydro- = water, -lysis = splitting). Denaturation only unfolds a protein; it does not break peptide bonds.

questions.q: Which bonds or interactions are responsible for each level of protein structure?
choices: Primary: hydrogen bonds. Secondary: peptide bonds. Tertiary: phosphodiester bonds. Quaternary: ester bonds.
Primary: peptide bonds. Secondary: hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms. Tertiary: interactions among R groups. Quaternary: interactions between separate polypeptides.
All four levels are held together only by peptide bonds.
Primary: disulfide bonds. Secondary: ionic bonds between R groups. Tertiary: peptide bonds. Quaternary: none.
questions.explain: The sequence (primary) is set by covalent peptide bonds. Helices and sheets (secondary) come from backbone hydrogen bonding, overall 3D folding (tertiary) from side-chain interactions, and multi-subunit assembly from interactions between chains.

questions.q: How do an alpha helix and a beta pleated sheet differ?
choices: An alpha helix is held by disulfide bridges; a beta sheet is held by peptide bonds.
An alpha helix forms between two different polypeptides only; a beta sheet is quaternary structure.
They are the same structure viewed from different angles.
An alpha helix is a coil stabilized by hydrogen bonds within one stretch of backbone; a beta sheet forms when separate, extended segments lie side by side and hydrogen bond to each other.
questions.explain: Both are secondary structures based on backbone hydrogen bonds; the difference is the geometry, coiled versus side-by-side strands. Disulfide bridges involve cysteine R groups and contribute to tertiary structure.

questions.q: Which factors promote protein folding and stability in tertiary structure?
choices: Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic effects, van der Waals forces, and disulfide bridges
Only peptide bonds
Only phosphodiester bonds and ester bonds
Only hydrogen bonds between bases
questions.explain: These five factors stabilize the 3D fold. Disulfide bridges are covalent links between two cysteine –SH groups; the rest are noncovalent interactions.

questions.q: What is quaternary structure?
choices: The association of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) into one functional protein
The amino acid sequence of a single polypeptide
The coiling of a single chain into an alpha helix
The final 3D folding of a single polypeptide
questions.explain: Tertiary is the final level for one chain; quaternary requires multiple subunits, which can be identical copies or different polypeptides.

questions.q: When a protein is denatured, for example by high heat, what happens?
choices: Its peptide bonds break, releasing free amino acids.
Its amino acid sequence is rearranged.
It becomes more active because it is more flexible.
Its hydrogen bonds and other interactions that maintain shape are disrupted, so it unfolds and loses function, while peptide bonds and primary structure remain intact.
questions.explain: Denaturation destroys secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, and because shape determines function, activity is lost. Breaking peptide bonds would be hydrolysis, not denaturation.

questions.q: In a mutant insulin, an amino acid with a nonpolar side chain is replaced by one with a polar side chain at a key position, and the overall shape of the hormone changes. What would you predict?
choices: The mutant insulin may not bind its receptor properly, so it would not lower blood glucose normally.
It would work normally, because only the primary structure changed.
It would work better, because polar amino acids are always more active.
It would be converted into glycogen.
questions.explain: One amino acid change can alter folding, and a protein's function depends on its shape. Saying 'only the primary structure changed' misses that primary structure determines all higher levels.

questions.q: In a protein, serine (polar, uncharged) is replaced by threonine (also polar, uncharged, and similar in size). What effect would you predict on the overall shape?
choices: A complete loss of structure, because any change destroys a protein.
Conversion of the protein into a lipid.
Little change, because the side chains have similar size and polarity.
Loss of all peptide bonds after the substitution.
questions.explain: Substituting a chemically similar amino acid usually preserves interactions and folding. Changes between categories, such as nonpolar to charged, are much more likely to disrupt structure.

questions.q: Which pairs a protein function category with a correct example?
choices: Storage: carrying genetic information
Enzymes: catalyzing reactions (such as catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide)
Motor: forming the plasma membrane bilayer
Transport: catalyzing peptide bond formation in the ribosome
questions.explain: Protein roles include enzymes, structure, transport, motors, storage, signaling, receptors, and gene regulation. Genetic information is stored in nucleic acids, the bilayer is made of lipids, and peptide bonds are catalyzed by rRNA.

questions.q: Which functional group is nonpolar?
choices: Hydroxyl (–OH)
Carboxyl (–COOH)
Methyl (–CH₃)
Amino (–NH₂)
questions.explain: The methyl group contains only C–H bonds, which share electrons nearly equally. Hydroxyl, carboxyl, and amino groups contain electronegative O or N, which makes them polar and able to hydrogen bond.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the acid-base behavior of the amino and carboxyl groups?
choices: Both groups are nonpolar and do not interact with H⁺.
The amino group is acidic, and the carboxyl group is basic.
Both groups are strongly basic.
The carboxyl group is acidic (it can donate H⁺), and the amino group is weakly basic (it can accept H⁺).
questions.explain: These are the two groups that join in a peptide bond. Their tendency to give up or accept H⁺ is also why amino acids with extra carboxyl or amino groups in their R groups are charged.

questions.q: A protein region binds a signaling molecule while a separate region binds DNA. What does this suggest about protein organization?
choices: Every protein has only one function.
DNA-binding requires quaternary structure in all cases.
Signaling molecules always bind the DNA directly.
Proteins can contain distinct functional domains, each with its own structure and function.
questions.explain: Nuclear receptors, for example, have separate ligand-binding, DNA-binding, nuclear localization, and activation domains. Proteins that share a domain tend to share the matching function.

questions.q: A disulfide bridge forms between two cysteines that are far apart in the amino acid sequence. Which level of structure does this most directly stabilize?
choices: Primary structure
Tertiary structure
Secondary structure only
No level, because disulfide bridges are not covalent
questions.explain: Disulfide bridges are covalent links between cysteine R groups that lock distant parts of the folded chain together, stabilizing the 3D (tertiary) fold. They do not create the sequence itself.

questions.q: How do kinetic energy and potential energy differ?
choices: Kinetic energy is the energy of movement; potential energy is stored energy due to structure or location, such as in chemical bonds.
Kinetic energy is stored in chemical bonds; potential energy is the energy of motion.
They are the same thing, measured in different units.
Potential energy exists only in living things.
questions.explain: Water flowing through a dam is kinetic energy, and water held behind it is potential energy. Chemical potential energy in bonds (in glucose, for example) is the main form cells use.

questions.q: What does the first law of thermodynamics state?
choices: Energy transfers always decrease the entropy of the universe.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
Living things create energy from nothing.
Energy can be destroyed when it becomes heat.
questions.explain: This is the law of conservation of energy. Energy released as heat is not destroyed; it is less useful to the cell, which is the subject of the second law.

questions.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics imply for living cells?
choices: Energy transfers are 100% efficient.
Each energy transfer increases entropy (disorder), so less energy is available to do work.
Entropy always decreases as energy is converted.
Cells can reuse heat as efficiently as chemical energy.
questions.explain: Some energy is always lost as unusable energy (often heat) during conversions. That is why organisms need a continual input of energy.

questions.q: In the equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what does a negative ΔG mean?
choices: The products have more free energy, so the reaction requires energy input.
The reaction happens instantly.
The products have less free energy than the reactants, so the reaction is exergonic and spontaneous.
The reaction cannot happen in a cell.
questions.explain: A negative ΔG means energy is released and the reaction is spontaneous, although spontaneous does not mean fast. Without an enzyme it might still be very slow.

questions.q: A reaction has a positive ΔG. Which statement is true?
choices: It is endergonic, not spontaneous, and needs an input of energy; its products store more free energy than its reactants.
It is exergonic and releases free energy.
It is spontaneous and will happen without help.
Its products have less free energy than its reactants.
questions.explain: Positive ΔG means energy must be added, often by coupling to ATP hydrolysis. Products of endergonic reactions, such as sugars from photosynthesis, hold more energy than the reactants did.

questions.q: Is cellular respiration (breaking down glucose to CO₂ and water) endergonic or exergonic?
choices: Endergonic: it requires a constant input of light energy.
Endergonic: its products store more energy than glucose.
Neither: respiration does not involve energy changes.
Exergonic: it releases free energy because the products have less free energy than glucose and oxygen.
questions.explain: Respiration is catabolic and exergonic: breaking glucose's bonds releases energy that cells capture as ATP. Photosynthesis is the reverse, endergonic and anabolic, and is powered by light.

questions.q: Photosynthesis builds glucose from CO₂ and water using light energy. How is it classified?
choices: Exergonic and catabolic
Endergonic and anabolic
Exergonic and anabolic
Endergonic and catabolic
questions.explain: Building larger, energy-rich molecules from smaller ones requires energy input (endergonic) and is a synthesis process (anabolic). Breakdown processes are catabolic and exergonic.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Catabolic pathways break molecules down and are exergonic; anabolic pathways build molecules and are endergonic.
Catabolic pathways build molecules and are endergonic.
Anabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy.
Both are always endergonic.
questions.explain: Metabolism is the sum of both. Anabolic (building) pathways must be coupled to exergonic reactions to proceed.

questions.q: How does an exothermic reaction differ from an endothermic one?
choices: Exothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings.
Exothermic reactions release heat, and the products have less potential energy (ΔH is negative); endothermic reactions take up heat, and the products have more potential energy.
Endothermic reactions always have a negative ΔG.
They differ in entropy only, not in heat.
questions.explain: Enthalpy (H) is the heat content, mostly the energy in bonds. Endothermic versus exothermic describes ΔH, while endergonic versus exergonic describes ΔG, which also includes entropy.

questions.q: Why does hydrolysis of ATP release so much free energy?
choices: Its three phosphate groups are negatively charged and repel each other, so breaking off the outer phosphate to form ADP + Pi is highly exergonic (about −7.3 kcal/mol).
ATP's phosphates are positively charged and attract each other strongly.
Hydrolysis of ATP forms new peptide bonds.
ATP is a lipid that stores energy in fatty acid tails.
questions.explain: Bonding three closely packed negative phosphates stores a lot of potential energy, and removing the outer phosphate relieves that strain. That is why ATP serves as the cell's energy currency.

questions.q: What is energetic coupling?
choices: Linking two endergonic reactions so that both release energy
Converting heat directly into chemical energy
Using the energy released by an exergonic reaction, such as ATP hydrolysis, to drive an endergonic reaction
Pairing a reaction with its enzyme's inhibitor
questions.explain: Coupling works when the combined ΔG is negative. ATP hydrolysis is the most common partner for driving otherwise unfavorable reactions.

questions.q: How does ATP provide energy for muscle contraction?
choices: ATP is burned like fuel to produce heat that expands the muscle.
ATP hydrolysis is coupled to shape changes in motor proteins, so the energy released drives the protein movements that shorten the muscle.
ATP bonds directly to actin and becomes part of the filament.
ATP is converted into glucose, which pulls the filaments together.
questions.explain: Contraction is endergonic work. Coupling it to exergonic ATP hydrolysis through motor protein conformational changes supplies the energy. Heat is a byproduct, not the mechanism.

questions.q: In a redox reaction, what happens to the molecule that is oxidized and to the one that is reduced?
choices: The oxidized molecule loses electrons; the reduced molecule gains electrons.
The oxidized molecule gains electrons; the reduced molecule loses them.
Both molecules gain oxygen atoms.
Neither molecule changes; only protons move.
questions.explain: Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. In the lecture, oxidation is the exergonic half-reaction and reduction the endergonic half, coupled together.

questions.q: What does it mean that a reaction is 'spontaneous'?
choices: It happens instantly.
It requires ATP to proceed.
Its products have more free energy than its reactants.
It has a negative ΔG and can proceed without an input of energy, although it may still be very slow.
questions.explain: Spontaneity describes direction, not speed. Many spontaneous reactions need an enzyme to occur at a useful rate because of their activation energy.

questions.q: What is an enzyme?
choices: A lipid that stores energy for the cell
A protein catalyst that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up
A molecule that is consumed in each reaction it speeds up
Any substance that raises the activation energy of a reaction
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They are reused many times, are specific for their substrates, and lower activation energy rather than raising it. RNA catalysts are called ribozymes.

questions.q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
choices: By making ΔG more negative
By supplying heat to the reactants
By changing the products of the reaction
By lowering the activation energy needed to reach the transition state
questions.explain: An enzyme stabilizes the transition state so that less energy is needed to reach it. It does not change ΔG or the products, which is the most commonly missed point.

questions.q: On an energy diagram, an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is compared with the same reaction without the enzyme. What differs?
choices: The products end at a lower free energy with the enzyme.
The reactants start at a higher free energy with the enzyme.
The reaction becomes endergonic with the enzyme.
The peak (activation energy) is lower with the enzyme, but the starting and ending free energies are the same.
questions.explain: Catalysts change the path, not the endpoints, so ΔG is unchanged. Only the height of the activation-energy barrier drops.

questions.q: What is induced fit?
choices: When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape to grip it more tightly, straining bonds toward the transition state.
The substrate changes shape to match a rigid active site.
The enzyme is permanently consumed in the reaction.
An inhibitor forces the active site closed.
questions.explain: For example, glucokinase closes around glucose and ATP once they bind. The active site is flexible rather than a rigid lock, which is the main difference from the older 'lock and key' idea.

questions.q: In an experiment, enzyme concentration is held constant while substrate concentration is increased. How does the reaction rate behave?
choices: It rises forever in a straight line.
It rises roughly linearly at low substrate levels, then levels off at a maximum when the enzyme is saturated.
It falls as substrate is added.
It stays constant at all substrate levels.
questions.explain: At saturation, nearly every active site is occupied, so adding more substrate cannot increase the rate. Only more enzyme would raise the maximum.

questions.q: What do 'affinity' and 'saturation' mean for an enzyme?
choices: Affinity is the maximum rate; saturation is the activation energy.
Affinity is how strongly the enzyme attracts its substrate; saturation is the plateau where nearly all active sites are occupied.
Affinity is the enzyme's optimal temperature; saturation is its optimal pH.
Both describe how much product is made.
questions.explain: The Michaelis constant (Km), the substrate concentration at half the maximum rate, is inversely related to affinity: a high Km means low affinity, so more substrate is needed.

questions.q: Enzyme X reaches half its maximum rate at 2 mM substrate, while enzyme Y needs 20 mM. Which has the higher affinity for its substrate?
choices: Enzyme Y, because it has the higher Km
Both are equal, because affinity does not depend on Km
Enzyme X, because it has the lower Km
Neither, because affinity applies only to inhibitors
questions.explain: Km is inversely related to affinity. An enzyme that gets to half its maximum rate at a lower substrate concentration binds its substrate more readily.

questions.q: How does a competitive inhibitor work?
choices: It binds an allosteric site and changes the enzyme's shape, lowering the maximum rate regardless of substrate.
It permanently destroys the enzyme's peptide bonds.
It resembles the substrate and binds the active site, blocking substrate binding; adding more substrate can overcome it.
It increases the enzyme's affinity for the substrate.
questions.explain: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site, so high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor. The apparent Km rises, but the maximum rate is unchanged. Binding at an allosteric site describes noncompetitive inhibition.

questions.q: A noncompetitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. What happens to the maximum rate, and does adding more substrate restore it?
choices: The maximum rate is unchanged, and adding substrate overcomes the inhibitor.
The maximum rate decreases, and adding more substrate does not restore it, because the inhibitor binds an allosteric site.
The maximum rate increases.
The inhibitor competes for the active site, so excess substrate fully restores the rate.
questions.explain: Noncompetitive inhibitors change the enzyme's shape from another site, effectively removing working enzyme. That lowers the maximum rate without changing Km, so extra substrate cannot fix it.

questions.q: Which contrast between an active site and an allosteric site is correct?
choices: The active site binds the substrate where catalysis happens; an allosteric site is elsewhere and binds regulators that change the enzyme's shape and activity.
The allosteric site binds the substrate; the active site binds regulators.
Both sites bind only competitive inhibitors.
Allosteric sites exist only in ribozymes.
questions.explain: Allosteric regulators can either activate the enzyme, by opening the active site, or inhibit it, by closing it, all without occupying the active site.

questions.q: Which correctly distinguishes cofactors, coenzymes, and prosthetic groups?
choices: Cofactors are proteins; coenzymes are lipids; prosthetic groups are RNA.
All three are types of competitive inhibitors.
Coenzymes are inorganic ions; cofactors are vitamins.
Cofactors are inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺; coenzymes are organic molecules, often from vitamins; prosthetic groups are non-protein parts permanently or tightly attached to the enzyme.
questions.explain: These helpers assist catalysis, for example by carrying electrons or stabilizing charges. Without them, many enzymes are inactive.

questions.q: What are ribozymes?
choices: Proteins that make ribosomes
RNA molecules that act as catalysts, such as the rRNA that forms peptide bonds in the ribosome
Enzymes that digest RNA only
DNA sequences that bind repressors
questions.explain: Not all biological catalysts are proteins. The ribosome's large subunit is a ribozyme.

questions.q: A human enzyme works best at 37 °C and pH 7. What happens if it is heated to 70 °C?
choices: Its activity keeps rising, because heat always speeds reactions.
It changes the ΔG of the reaction it catalyzes.
It becomes a ribozyme.
Its activity drops sharply because the heat denatures it and disrupts the shape of its active site.
questions.explain: Enzymes work within a narrow range of conditions. Moderate warming speeds collisions, but beyond the optimum, bonds that hold the 3D shape break and the active site no longer fits the substrate.

questions.q: What is feedback inhibition in a metabolic pathway?
choices: The end product of the pathway inhibits an enzyme early in the pathway, preventing over-accumulation of the product.
The first substrate activates the final enzyme.
The product stimulates its own production without limit.
Every enzyme in the pathway is inhibited by the first reactant.
questions.explain: This is negative feedback, which keeps product levels steady. Positive feedback is the opposite: the product stimulates more of its own production.

questions.q: In pathway A → B → C → D, the conversion of B to C is the slowest (rate-limiting) step. Where would regulation have the greatest effect on the output of D?
choices: At the enzyme that converts C to D
At no enzyme, because pathways cannot be regulated
At the enzyme that converts B to C
Equally at every step
questions.explain: Speeding up or slowing the rate-limiting step changes the whole pathway's output most. Regulating a fast step barely matters, because material still piles up at the slow step.

questions.q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
choices: A reaction's product inhibits the first enzyme in its pathway.
An enzyme is denatured by high temperature.
A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site.
A reaction's product stimulates the enzyme that makes it, so production accelerates.
questions.explain: In positive feedback, the output amplifies itself. Negative feedback, where the product slows its own production, is far more common for keeping metabolism stable.

questions.q: A drug closely resembles an enzyme's normal substrate. Which kind of inhibition is it most likely to cause, and how could the effect be reduced?
choices: Noncompetitive inhibition; raising the substrate concentration would have no effect.
Allosteric activation; the enzyme would speed up.
Competitive inhibition; raising the substrate concentration would reduce the effect.
Denaturation; cooling the enzyme would reverse it.
questions.explain: Structural similarity to the substrate lets the drug occupy the active site. Because the two molecules compete, flooding the system with substrate outcompetes the inhibitor.

questions.q: Which statement about enzyme specificity is correct?
choices: Each enzyme catalyzes every reaction in the cell.
Specificity comes from the enzyme being consumed by its substrate.
Each enzyme acts on particular substrates because the shape and chemistry of its active site fit only certain molecules.
Enzymes recognize substrates only by size, not shape or chemistry.
questions.explain: Shape determines function: the arrangement of R groups in the active site binds specific substrates. Catalase, for instance, acts on hydrogen peroxide.
